nodes.name: Riemann Hypothesis
nodes.statement: Every non-trivial zero of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s) has real part 1/2.
nodes.by: Bernhard Riemann, 1859
nodes.note: Levent Alpöge released a proof as a Lean library of about 17 million lines on 20 Nov 2026. The Lean FRO and Mathlib Initiative certified it on 21 Nov 2026. Human review of the ideas is still pending.

nodes.name: Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (Dirichlet L-functions)
nodes.statement: Every zero of every Dirichlet L-function L(s, χ) inside the critical strip has real part 1/2.
nodes.by: Adolf Piltz, 1884
nodes.note: Contains the Riemann Hypothesis as the special case of the trivial character.

nodes.name: Extended Riemann Hypothesis (Dedekind zeta functions)
nodes.statement: For every number field K, every zero of the Dedekind zeta function ζ_K(s) inside the critical strip has real part 1/2.
nodes.by: The Riemann Hypothesis carried over to the zeta functions Dedekind defined for number fields
nodes.note: Implies GRH for Dirichlet L-functions, because the zeta function of a cyclotomic field is a product of Dirichlet L-functions.

nodes.name: Riemann Hypothesis for modular-form L-functions
nodes.statement: Every zero of the L-function of a Hecke newform inside its critical strip lies on the central line.
nodes.by: Part of the Grand Riemann Hypothesis

nodes.name: Montgomery's pair correlation conjecture
nodes.statement: The spacings between zeros of ζ(s) on the critical line follow the pair correlation density 1 − (sin(πu)/(πu))², the same as eigenvalues of random Hermitian matrices.
nodes.by: Hugh Montgomery, 1973
nodes.note: Describes how the zeros are spaced along the line. The Riemann Hypothesis only says they are on the line.

nodes.name: Linear independence hypothesis
nodes.statement: The positive imaginary parts of the zeros of Dirichlet L-functions are linearly independent over the rational numbers.
nodes.by: Aurel Wintner, 1935 (for ζ); used for Dirichlet L-functions by Rubinstein and Sarnak, 1994

nodes.name: Legendre's conjecture
nodes.statement: There is a prime between n² and (n+1)² for every positive integer n.
nodes.by: Adrien-Marie Legendre, 1808
nodes.note: The Riemann Hypothesis gives prime gaps of size O(√p · log p). Legendre's conjecture needs gaps below about 2√p, so the Riemann Hypothesis falls just short.

nodes.name: Cramér's conjecture
nodes.statement: p(n+1) − p(n) = O(log² p(n)): gaps between consecutive primes are at most of the order of the squared logarithm.
nodes.by: Harald Cramér, 1936
nodes.note: Far stronger than what the Riemann Hypothesis gives.

nodes.name: Von Koch's error term for the prime number theorem
nodes.statement: π(x) = li(x) + O(√x · log x).
nodes.by: Helge von Koch, 1901

nodes.name: Growth of the Mertens function
nodes.statement: M(x) = O(x^(1/2+ε)) for every ε > 0, where M(x) is the sum of the Möbius function μ(n) for n ≤ x.
nodes.by: J. E. Littlewood, 1912

nodes.name: Robin's inequality
nodes.statement: σ(n) < e^γ · n · log log n for every n > 5040, where σ(n) is the sum of the divisors of n.
nodes.by: Guy Robin, 1984

nodes.name: Lagarias's inequality
nodes.statement: σ(n) ≤ H(n) + e^H(n) · log H(n) for every n ≥ 1, where H(n) is the n-th harmonic number.
nodes.by: Jeffrey Lagarias, 2002

nodes.name: Li's criterion
nodes.statement: λ(n) ≥ 0 for every n ≥ 1, where λ(n) is the sum of 1 − (1 − 1/ρ)^n over the non-trivial zeros ρ of ζ(s).
nodes.by: Xian-Jin Li, 1997

nodes.name: Nicolas's criterion
nodes.statement: N / φ(N) > e^γ · log log N for every primorial N, where φ is Euler's totient function.
nodes.by: Jean-Louis Nicolas, 1983

nodes.name: Franel–Landau theorem on Farey sequences
nodes.statement: The Farey fractions of order n deviate from equally spaced points by a total of O(n^(1/2+ε)).
nodes.by: Jérôme Franel and Edmund Landau, 1924

nodes.name: De Bruijn–Newman constant equals zero
nodes.statement: The de Bruijn–Newman constant Λ equals 0.
nodes.by: N. G. de Bruijn, 1950; Charles Newman, 1976
nodes.note: The Riemann Hypothesis is equivalent to Λ ≤ 0. Rodgers and Tao proved Λ ≥ 0 in 2018, so together Λ = 0.

nodes.name: Speiser's criterion
nodes.statement: The derivative ζ′(s) has no zeros in the strip 0 < Re(s) < 1/2.
nodes.by: Andreas Speiser, 1934

nodes.name: Schoenfeld's explicit prime-counting bound
nodes.statement: |π(x) − li(x)| < √x · log x / (8π) for every x ≥ 2657.
nodes.by: Lowell Schoenfeld, 1976

nodes.name: Cramér's prime gap bound
nodes.statement: p(n+1) − p(n) = O(√p(n) · log p(n)).
nodes.by: Harald Cramér, 1920

nodes.name: Explicit primes in short intervals
nodes.statement: For every x ≥ 2 there is a prime p with x − (4/π) · √x · log x < p ≤ x.
nodes.by: Adrian Dudek, 2015

nodes.name: Littlewood's bound for ζ on the critical line
nodes.statement: |ζ(1/2 + it)| ≤ exp(C · log t / log log t) for some constant C and all large t.
nodes.by: J. E. Littlewood, 1924

nodes.name: Lindelöf hypothesis
nodes.statement: ζ(1/2 + it) = O(t^ε) for every ε > 0.
nodes.by: Ernst Lindelöf, 1908
nodes.note: Littlewood's bound grows more slowly than any power of t, so it gives the Lindelöf hypothesis at once.

nodes.name: Density hypothesis
nodes.statement: N(σ, T) = O(T^(2(1−σ)+ε)), where N(σ, T) counts zeros of ζ(s) with real part at least σ and imaginary part up to T.
nodes.by: A. E. Ingham, 1937 (showed it follows from the Lindelöf hypothesis)

nodes.name: Prime number theorem in short intervals
nodes.short: Prime number theorem in short intervals
nodes.statement: π(x + x^θ) − π(x) ~ x^θ / log x for every θ > 1/2.
nodes.by: Follows from the density hypothesis (Ingham's method, 1937)
nodes.note: Also follows from the Riemann Hypothesis directly. Shown here as the end of the chain through Lindelöf and the density hypothesis.

nodes.name: Two thirds of the zeros are simple
nodes.statement: At least 2/3 of the non-trivial zeros of ζ(s) are simple.
nodes.by: Hugh Montgomery, 1973
nodes.note: An August 2026 preprint by Alpöge and Furman claims this without assuming the hypothesis.

nodes.name: Selberg's primes in almost all short intervals
nodes.short: Primes in almost all short intervals
nodes.statement: If f(x) → ∞, then almost all intervals [x, x + f(x) · log² x] contain a prime.
nodes.by: Atle Selberg, 1943

nodes.name: Goldston–Heath-Brown prime gap bound
nodes.by: Roger Heath-Brown and Daniel Goldston, 1984

nodes.name: Almost all zeros are simple
nodes.statement: The simple zeros of ζ(s) make up 100% of all its non-trivial zeros.
nodes.by: P. X. Gallagher and Julia Mueller, 1978 (conjectured by Montgomery, 1973)
nodes.note: Follows from the pair correlation conjecture alone. The Riemann Hypothesis by itself only gives two thirds.

nodes.name: Ankeny's bound for the least quadratic non-residue
nodes.statement: The least quadratic non-residue modulo a prime p is O(log² p).
nodes.by: Nesmith Ankeny, 1952

nodes.name: Vinogradov's conjecture on the least non-residue
nodes.statement: The least quadratic non-residue modulo p is O(p^ε) for every ε > 0.
nodes.by: I. M. Vinogradov

nodes.name: Miller's deterministic primality test
nodes.statement: Miller's test decides whether n is prime, without randomness, in time polynomial in log n.
nodes.by: Gary Miller, 1976
nodes.note: Miller's analysis needs a small witness for every composite n. The hypothesis for quadratic characters guarantees one of size O(log² n).

nodes.name: Deterministic square roots modulo a prime
nodes.statement: Square roots modulo a prime p can be computed without randomness in time polynomial in log p.
nodes.by: Tonelli–Shanks algorithm with Ankeny's bound
nodes.note: The Tonelli–Shanks algorithm needs one quadratic non-residue. Ankeny's bound guarantees that trying 2, 3, 4, … finds one quickly.

nodes.name: Bach's explicit witness bound
nodes.statement: Every proper subgroup of the units modulo n misses some integer below 2 · ln² n. So n is prime exactly when it passes the strong pseudoprime test for every base up to 2 · ln² n.
nodes.by: Eric Bach, 1990

nodes.name: Least prime in an arithmetic progression
nodes.statement: For coprime a and q with q > 3, the least prime p ≡ a (mod q) is at most (φ(q) · log q)².
nodes.by: Youness Lamzouri, Xiannan Li and Kannan Soundararajan, 2015

nodes.name: Shoup's bound for the least primitive root
nodes.statement: The least primitive root modulo a prime p is O(log⁶ p).
nodes.by: Victor Shoup, 1992

nodes.name: Littlewood's bounds for L(1, χ)
nodes.statement: L(1, χ) ≤ (2 + o(1)) · e^γ · log log q for every primitive real character χ modulo q.
nodes.by: J. E. Littlewood, 1928
nodes.note: Through the class number formula this bounds class numbers of quadratic fields.

nodes.name: Euler's list of idoneal numbers is complete
nodes.statement: There are exactly 65 idoneal numbers, the ones Euler found, the largest being 1848.
nodes.by: Peter Weinberger, 1973
nodes.note: Without the hypothesis, Weinberger's results imply that at most two more idoneal numbers can exist.

nodes.name: Chebyshev's bias, quantified
nodes.statement: Primes of the form 4k+3 are ahead of primes of the form 4k+1 for a set of x of logarithmic density about 0.9959.
nodes.by: Michael Rubinstein and Peter Sarnak, 1994

nodes.name: Ramanujan's ternary quadratic form
nodes.statement: The form x² + y² + 10z² represents every odd integer greater than 2719.
nodes.by: Ken Ono and Kannan Soundararajan, 1997

nodes.name: Artin's conjecture on primitive roots
nodes.statement: Every integer a that is neither −1 nor a perfect square is a primitive root modulo infinitely many primes, and these primes have a positive density that is a rational multiple of Artin's constant.
nodes.by: Christopher Hooley, 1967
nodes.note: Preprints from October and November 2026 claim the "infinitely many primes" part without the hypothesis. The density is still only known through Hooley's conditional proof.

nodes.name: Weinberger's theorem on Euclidean number rings
nodes.statement: If the ring of integers of a number field has infinitely many units, it is Euclidean exactly when it has class number 1.
nodes.by: Peter Weinberger, 1973

nodes.name: Effective Chebotarev density theorem
nodes.statement: In a Galois extension L of the rationals, every conjugacy class of the Galois group is the Frobenius class of a prime p = O((log |d_L|)²), where d_L is the discriminant of L.
nodes.by: Jeffrey Lagarias and Andrew Odlyzko, 1977

nodes.name: Bach's bound for class group generators
nodes.statement: The class group of a number field K is generated by the prime ideals of norm at most 12 · log² |Δ|, where Δ is the discriminant of K.
nodes.by: Eric Bach, 1990
nodes.note: The unconditional Minkowski bound grows like √|Δ|, which is far too large for big fields.

nodes.name: Class groups computed assuming the hypothesis
nodes.statement: Class groups and unit groups from PARI/GP's bnfinit, from SageMath with proof=False, from Magma with Proof := "GRH", and the LMFDB number-field entries flagged as conditional, are correct.
nodes.by: PARI/GP, LMFDB (SageMath and Magma on request)
nodes.note: PARI/GP assumes the hypothesis by default and only searches prime ideals up to a bound it justifies, until the result is certified with bnfcertify. SageMath and Magma do so only when asked.

nodes.name: Ternary Goldbach theorem
nodes.statement: Every odd integer greater than 5 is the sum of three primes.
nodes.by: Harald Helfgott, 2013
nodes.note: First proven assuming GRH (Deshouillers, Effinger, te Riele and Zinoviev, 1997). Helfgott's proof removed the hypothesis.

nodes.name: Primality testing in polynomial time
nodes.statement: Whether n is prime can be decided without randomness in time polynomial in log n.
nodes.by: Manindra Agrawal, Neeraj Kayal and Nitin Saxena, 2002
nodes.note: Known since 1976 assuming GRH, through Miller's test. The AKS test removed the hypothesis.

nodes.name: Prime number theorem
nodes.statement: The number π(x) of primes up to x is asymptotic to x / log x: the ratio of the two tends to 1 as x grows.
nodes.by: Jacques Hadamard and Charles Jean de la Vallée Poussin, independently, 1896
nodes.note: The proofs rest on the fact that ζ(s) has no zeros on the line Re(s) = 1. The Riemann Hypothesis would give the much sharper error term in von Koch's theorem.

nodes.name: Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions
nodes.statement: If a and d are coprime positive integers, the progression a, a + d, a + 2d, … contains infinitely many primes.
nodes.by: Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet, 1837
nodes.note: The proof introduced Dirichlet L-functions. Its key step is that L(1, χ) is not zero for every non-trivial character χ.

nodes.name: Siegel–Walfisz theorem
nodes.statement: For moduli q up to any fixed power (log x)^N, the primes up to x are shared out almost exactly evenly among the residue classes modulo q that are coprime to q, with an error of order x · exp(−c · √(log x)), where c > 0 depends only on N.
nodes.by: Arnold Walfisz, 1936, applying a theorem of Carl Ludwig Siegel
nodes.note: A refinement of both the prime number theorem and Dirichlet's theorem. The constants cannot be computed, because Siegel's theorem is ineffective.

nodes.name: Chebotarev density theorem
nodes.statement: Let L be a finite Galois extension of the rational numbers with Galois group G. For each conjugacy class C of G, the primes p not dividing the discriminant whose Frobenius element lies in C make up a proportion |C| / |G| of all primes.
nodes.by: Nikolai Chebotaryov, 1922 (published 1926)
nodes.note: Dirichlet's theorem is the special case of cyclotomic fields. A bound for the least prime in each class of order (log of the discriminant)² is known only under the extended Riemann hypothesis (Lagarias and Odlyzko).

nodes.name: Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem
nodes.statement: On average over the moduli q up to about √x, the primes up to x are spread among the residue classes modulo q about as evenly as the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis would give for each single q.
nodes.by: Enrico Bombieri and A. I. Vinogradov, independently, 1965
nodes.note: Often called GRH on average. The proof handles small moduli with the Siegel–Walfisz theorem and large moduli with the large sieve (R. C. Vaughan's notes, linked on the dependency).

nodes.name: Vinogradov's three primes theorem
nodes.statement: Every sufficiently large odd integer is the sum of three primes.
nodes.by: I. M. Vinogradov, 1937
nodes.note: Hardy and Littlewood proved it in 1923 assuming the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. Vinogradov's proof used the ineffective Siegel–Walfisz theorem, so it gave no explicit threshold. Helfgott's 2013 ternary Goldbach theorem covers every odd number above 5.

nodes.name: Goldbach's conjecture
nodes.statement: Every even integer greater than 2 is the sum of two primes.
nodes.by: Christian Goldbach, in a letter to Leonhard Euler, 1742
nodes.note: It implies the ternary Goldbach theorem, but not the other way round. Checked by computer for all even numbers up to 4 × 10¹⁸ (2013).

nodes.name: Generalized Elliott–Halberstam conjecture
nodes.statement: The even spreading of primes among residue classes that the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture predicts, on average over moduli up to x^θ for every θ < 1, also holds for a wide class of products (Dirichlet convolutions) of two sequences.
nodes.by: Enrico Bombieri, John Friedlander and Henryk Iwaniec, 1986
nodes.note: Motohashi proved the range θ < 1/2, a generalized Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem.

nodes.name: Elliott–Halberstam conjecture
nodes.statement: For every θ < 1, the primes up to x are spread evenly among residue classes, on average over all moduli q up to x^θ, with a total error smaller than x / (log x)^A for every A.
nodes.by: Peter Elliott and Heini Halberstam, 1968
nodes.note: The Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem proves it for θ < 1/2. It is known to fail at θ = 1. The Polymath paper (Proposition 2.7) shows the generalized form implies it.

nodes.name: Zhang's theorem on bounded gaps between primes
nodes.statement: There are infinitely many pairs of consecutive primes that differ by less than 70 million.
nodes.by: Yitang Zhang, 2013 (published 2014)
nodes.note: Goldston, Pintz and Yıldırım had shown in 2005 that the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture gives gaps of at most 16 infinitely often. Zhang proved a weaker version of that conjecture, for moduli without large prime factors slightly beyond √x, which was enough.

nodes.name: Maynard's theorem on primes in bounded intervals
nodes.statement: For every m there is a bound H such that infinitely many intervals of length H contain at least m primes. For m = 2, consecutive primes differ by at most 600 infinitely often.
nodes.by: James Maynard, 2013 (published 2015); related unpublished work by Terence Tao
nodes.note: Maynard's multidimensional sieve needs no information on primes beyond the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem, unlike Zhang's argument.

nodes.name: Prime gaps of at most 246
nodes.statement: There are infinitely many pairs of consecutive primes that differ by at most 246.
nodes.by: D. H. J. Polymath, 2014
nodes.note: 246 is the smallest bound in a refereed paper. The paper refines Maynard's sieve and states that this bound uses only the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem.
nodes.claim: Since August 2026 several unrefereed preprints have claimed smaller bounds, starting with Julia Stadlmann's 240. None had been independently verified by September 2026.

nodes.name: Prime gaps of at most 12, assuming Elliott–Halberstam
nodes.statement: There are infinitely many pairs of consecutive primes that differ by at most 12.
nodes.by: James Maynard, 2013

nodes.name: Prime gaps of at most 6, assuming generalized Elliott–Halberstam
nodes.statement: There are infinitely many pairs of consecutive primes that differ by at most 6.
nodes.by: D. H. J. Polymath, 2014
nodes.note: The parity problem rules out any bound below 6 by purely sieve-theoretic methods, so these methods cannot reach the twin prime conjecture even with this hypothesis.

nodes.name: Schinzel's hypothesis H
nodes.statement: If finitely many irreducible integer polynomials with positive leading coefficients have no fixed prime dividing the product of their values, then infinitely many integers n make all of them prime at once.
nodes.by: Andrzej Schinzel and Wacław Sierpiński, 1958
nodes.note: The only proven case is a single linear polynomial, which is Dirichlet's theorem. It also predicts infinitely many primes of the form n² + 1, one of Landau's problems.

nodes.name: Twin prime conjecture
nodes.statement: There are infinitely many primes p such that p + 2 is also prime.
nodes.by: Stated for every even gap by Alphonse de Polignac, 1849
nodes.note: Hypothesis H applied to n and n + 2 gives it at once. In terms of prime gaps it says that a gap of 2 occurs infinitely often. The smallest gap proven in a refereed paper to occur infinitely often is 246.

nodes.name: Modularity theorem for semistable elliptic curves
nodes.statement: Every semistable elliptic curve over the rational numbers is modular: it can be parametrized by a modular curve, and its L-function comes from a modular form.
nodes.by: Andrew Wiles, with Richard Taylor, 1995
nodes.note: Semistable means the curve has only the mildest kind of bad reduction at each prime. Wiles announced a proof in 1993; an error found that year was repaired in 1994, with one step justified in a joint paper with Taylor.

nodes.name: Ribet's theorem (epsilon conjecture)
nodes.statement: The elliptic curve that Gerhard Frey attached to a hypothetical solution of aᵖ + bᵖ = cᵖ, with p a prime of at least 5, cannot be modular.
nodes.by: Ken Ribet, 1986 (published 1990)
nodes.note: This was the epsilon conjecture, the missing step in an argument Jean-Pierre Serre gave in 1985. After it, the modularity of semistable curves was all that Fermat's Last Theorem needed.

nodes.name: Fermat's Last Theorem
nodes.statement: The equation aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ has no solution in positive integers a, b, c when n is greater than 2.
nodes.by: Andrew Wiles, 1995 (with Richard Taylor)
nodes.note: A counterexample with a prime exponent p ≥ 5 would give a semistable Frey curve (the exponents 3 and 4 were settled by Euler and Fermat). Ribet showed that curve is not modular, and Wiles showed every semistable curve is modular.

nodes.name: Modularity theorem
nodes.statement: Every elliptic curve over the rational numbers is modular: it is the image of a classical modular curve under a rational map with integer coefficients.
nodes.by: Christophe Breuil, Brian Conrad, Fred Diamond and Richard Taylor, 2001
nodes.note: Formerly the Taniyama–Shimura conjecture (1950s). The proof extended Wiles's techniques from semistable curves to all curves.

nodes.name: Serre's modularity conjecture (Khare–Wintenberger theorem)
nodes.statement: Every continuous, odd, absolutely irreducible two-dimensional representation of the absolute Galois group of the rational numbers, with coefficients in a finite field, comes from a modular form, of a level and weight that Serre specified.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Jean-Pierre Serre (1975, 1987); proved by Chandrashekhar Khare and Jean-Pierre Wintenberger, 2008 (published 2009)
nodes.note: Serre showed his conjecture implies Fermat's Last Theorem and the modularity theorem. Khare proved the level 1 case first, in 2005.

nodes.name: Faltings's theorem (Mordell conjecture)
nodes.statement: A non-singular curve of genus greater than 1 defined over the rational numbers has only finitely many rational points.
nodes.by: Gerd Faltings, 1983 (conjectured by Louis Mordell, 1922)
nodes.note: Known proofs bound the number of rational points but not their size, so they do not tell how to find them. Elkies showed in 1991 that the abc conjecture would also imply the theorem.

nodes.name: Darmon–Granville theorem
nodes.statement: For fixed exponents m, n, k with 1/m + 1/n + 1/k < 1, the equation aᵐ + bⁿ = cᵏ has only finitely many solutions in coprime positive integers a, b, c.
nodes.by: Henri Darmon and Andrew Granville, 1995
nodes.note: The Fermat–Catalan conjecture asks for more: finitely many solutions even when the exponents may vary.

nodes.name: abc conjecture
nodes.statement: For every ε > 0 there are only finitely many triples of coprime positive integers with a + b = c and c > rad(abc)^(1+ε), where rad(n) is the product of the distinct primes dividing n.
nodes.by: Joseph Oesterlé and David Masser, 1985
nodes.note: Shinichi Mochizuki claimed a proof in 2012, published in 2021. Peter Scholze and Jakob Stix reported a serious gap in 2018, and the mainstream community still regards the conjecture as unproven in November 2026.

nodes.name: Effective Mordell from the abc conjecture
nodes.statement: For every curve of genus at least 2 over the rational numbers, the size (height) of its rational points is bounded by an explicit constant, so all of them can be found by an algorithm.
nodes.by: Noam Elkies, 1991
nodes.note: Faltings's theorem shows the points are finitely many but gives no bound on their size. Elkies showed that a version of the abc conjecture with computable constants would give one.

nodes.name: Modified Szpiro conjecture
nodes.statement: For every ε > 0 there is a constant C(ε) such that every elliptic curve over the rationals satisfies max(|c₄|³, |c₆|²) ≤ C(ε) · N^(6+ε), where c₄ and c₆ are the invariants of a minimal Weierstrass equation and N is the conductor.
nodes.by: Lucien Szpiro, 1981; equivalence with abc shown by Joseph Oesterlé, 1988
nodes.note: The conductor records the primes where the curve has bad reduction. Szpiro's original form, which bounds the discriminant, follows from this one.

nodes.name: Fermat–Catalan conjecture
nodes.statement: The equation aᵐ + bⁿ = cᵏ with coprime positive integers a, b, c and 1/m + 1/n + 1/k < 1 has only finitely many solutions, counting distinct triples of powers.
nodes.by: Henri Darmon and Andrew Granville, 1995, who also observed that it follows from the abc conjecture
nodes.note: Ten solutions are known, for example 2⁵ + 7² = 3⁴.

nodes.name: Infinitely many non-Wieferich primes
nodes.statement: For every base b > 1 there are infinitely many primes p for which p² does not divide b^(p−1) − 1.
nodes.by: Joseph Silverman, 1988
nodes.note: Only two Wieferich primes to base 2 are known, 1093 and 3511, and any third one exceeds 2⁶⁴. Yet without the abc conjecture it is not even known that infinitely many primes are not Wieferich primes.

nodes.name: Mihăilescu's theorem (Catalan's conjecture)
nodes.statement: The only two consecutive perfect powers are 8 and 9: the equation xᵃ − yᵇ = 1 with a, b > 1 has the single solution in positive integers 3² − 2³ = 1.
nodes.by: Preda Mihăilescu, 2002 (published 2004); conjectured by Eugène Catalan, 1844
nodes.note: Tijdeman had shown in 1976 that there are only finitely many solutions. Mihăilescu's proof uses cyclotomic fields and Galois modules.

nodes.name: Gross–Zagier theorem
nodes.statement: For a modular elliptic curve E and a suitable imaginary quadratic field K, the height of a Heegner point equals, up to an explicit nonzero factor, the derivative at s = 1 of the L-function of E over K. Combined with the existence of a suitable K, this shows that if L(E, s) has a simple zero at s = 1, then E has a rational point of infinite order.
nodes.by: Benedict Gross and Don Zagier, 1986

nodes.name: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture for analytic rank 0 and 1
nodes.statement: For an elliptic curve over the rationals whose L-function does not vanish at s = 1, the group of rational points is finite. If the L-function has a simple zero there, the group has rank exactly 1.
nodes.by: Victor Kolyvagin, 1989, building on Gross and Zagier, 1986; extended to all curves by the modularity theorem, 2001
nodes.note: Kolyvagin built Euler systems from Heegner points. The results were stated for modular elliptic curves, so they covered every curve only once all curves were known to be modular.

nodes.name: Effective solution of Gauss's class number problem
nodes.statement: For each h, all imaginary quadratic fields with class number h can be listed by a finite calculation.
nodes.by: Dorian Goldfeld, 1976, completed by the Gross–Zagier theorem, 1986
nodes.note: Goldfeld reduced the problem to finding an elliptic curve whose L-function has a zero of high order at s = 1. The Gross–Zagier theorem supplied one.

nodes.name: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture
nodes.statement: The rank of the group of rational points of an elliptic curve E over the rationals equals the order of the zero of its L-function L(E, s) at s = 1.
nodes.by: Bryan Birch and Peter Swinnerton-Dyer, 1960s
nodes.note: One of the Clay Millennium Prize problems. No proof has been accepted as of November 2026.

nodes.name: Tunnell's criterion for congruent numbers
nodes.statement: For an odd squarefree integer n, write A for the number of integer solutions of 2x² + y² + 32z² = n and B for the number of 2x² + y² + 8z² = n (similar equations handle even n). If n is congruent, that is, the area of a right triangle with rational sides, then B = 2A. If the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture holds, the converse is also true.
nodes.by: Jerrold Tunnell, 1983
nodes.note: One direction is proven: every congruent number passes the test. That every number passing the test is congruent needs the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture for the curves y² = x³ − n²x.

nodes.name: Sato–Tate theorem
nodes.statement: For an elliptic curve over the rationals without complex multiplication, write its number of points modulo p as p + 1 − 2√p · cos θ_p. Then the angles θ_p are distributed over [0, π] with density proportional to sin² θ.
nodes.by: Laurent Clozel, Michael Harris, Nick Shepherd-Barron and Richard Taylor, 2008 (curves with multiplicative reduction at some prime); Thomas Barnet-Lamb, David Geraghty, Michael Harris and Richard Taylor, 2011 (in general)
nodes.note: Conjectured by Mikio Sato and John Tate around 1960. The proof rests on potential modularity results.

nodes.name: Effective abc conjecture
nodes.statement: For every ε > 0 the abc inequality c ≤ C(ε) · rad(abc)^(1+ε) holds for all coprime positive integers with a + b = c, with a constant C(ε) that can be computed.
nodes.by: Used by Noam Elkies, 1991
nodes.note: Stronger than the abc conjecture, which only says that some constant exists. A proof of abc with constants nobody can compute would not give the results that rest on this version.

nodes.name: Moessner's theorem
nodes.statement: Let n be a positive integer. Start from the positive integers 1, 2, 3, …, remove every n-th number and replace what remains by its running totals (partial sums). Then remove every (n−1)-st number of the new sequence and take running totals again, and so on, ending with a round that removes every second number; the sequence obtained is 1ⁿ, 2ⁿ, 3ⁿ, 4ⁿ, …
nodes.by: Alfred Moessner, 1951; first proof by Oskar Perron, 1951
nodes.note: For n = 2, removing every even number leaves 1, 3, 5, 7, … and the partial sums are 1, 4, 9, 16, … Removing the triangular numbers instead leads in a similar way to the factorials 1!, 2!, 3!, …

nodes.name: Apéry's theorem
nodes.statement: Apéry's constant ζ(3) = 1 + 1/2³ + 1/3³ + ⋯ = 1.2020569… is irrational: it cannot be written as a fraction p/q with p and q integers.
nodes.by: Roger Apéry, 1978
nodes.note: The values of the Riemann zeta function at positive even integers are irrational. Whether its values at the odd integers 2n+1 with n > 1 are irrational remains open, though they are conjectured to be.

nodes.name: Minkowski's theorem
nodes.statement: Every convex set in ℝⁿ that is symmetric about the origin and has volume greater than 2ⁿ contains a non-zero integer point. More generally, for a lattice L in ℝⁿ, a symmetric convex set with volume greater than 2ⁿ·d(L) contains a point of L other than the origin, where d(L) is the covolume of L.
nodes.by: Hermann Minkowski, 1889
nodes.note: The theorem became the foundation of the branch of number theory called the geometry of numbers.

nodes.name: Dedekind–Kummer theorem
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field with ring of algebraic integers O_K, let α ∈ O_K with ℚ[α] = K, and let f be the minimal polynomial of α over ℤ[x]. For any prime p not dividing the index [O_K : ℤ[α]], if f(x) ≡ π₁(x)^e₁ ⋯ π_g(x)^e_g mod p with π₁, …, π_g pairwise distinct monic irreducible polynomials in 𝔽_p[x], then the ideal pO_K factors into prime ideals as 𝔭₁^e₁ ⋯ 𝔭_g^e_g, where the ideal norm N(𝔭ᵢ) equals p raised to the degree of πᵢ.
nodes.by: Richard Dedekind, building on the work of Ernst Kummer
nodes.note: It describes how a prime ideal factors in a larger ring of integers. It holds more generally for a nonzero prime ideal of a Dedekind domain that is coprime to the conductor, in a finite separable extension generated by one element.

nodes.name: Lemoine's conjecture
nodes.statement: Every odd integer greater than 5 can be written as the sum of an odd prime and an even semiprime. Equivalently, 2n + 1 = p + 2q has a solution in primes p and q (not necessarily distinct) for every n > 2.
nodes.by: Émile Lemoine, 1895
nodes.note: MathWorld erroneously attributed it to Hyman Levy, hence the name Levy's conjecture. It implies Goldbach's weak conjecture and has been verified up to 10^9.

nodes.name: Bunyakovsky conjecture
nodes.statement: Let f(x) be a polynomial in one variable with integer coefficients such that its leading coefficient is positive, it is irreducible over the rationals, and the values f(1), f(2), f(3), … have no common factor larger than 1. Then f(n) is prime for infinitely many positive integers n.
nodes.by: Viktor Bunyakovsky, 1857
nodes.note: The three conditions are necessary for infinitely many prime values. Only the degree 1 case is proved, and that case is Dirichlet's theorem; the conjecture is a special case of Schinzel's hypothesis H.

nodes.name: Fermat polygonal number theorem
nodes.statement: For every n ≥ 3, every positive integer is a sum of at most n n-gonal numbers. For example, every positive integer is a sum of three or fewer triangular numbers and of four or fewer square numbers.
nodes.by: Stated by Pierre de Fermat, 1638, without proof; the square case was proved by Lagrange, 1770, the triangular case by Gauss, 1796, and the full theorem by Cauchy, 1813

nodes.name: Hall's conjecture
nodes.statement: For every ε > 0 there is a positive constant c(ε) such that for all integers x and y with y² ≠ x³, |y² − x³| > c(ε)·|x|^(1/2 − ε). In words, a square and a cube that are not equal lie far apart.
nodes.by: Original strong form by Marshall Hall, Jr., 1970; the weak form stated here by Stark and Trotter around 1980
nodes.note: The original strong form, with exponent 1/2 and a fixed constant C, has never been disproved but is no longer believed to be true. The weak form would follow from the ABC conjecture.

nodes.name: Lucas's theorem
nodes.statement: Let m and n be non-negative integers and p a prime, with base p expansions m = m_k·p^k + … + m₁·p + m₀ and n = n_k·p^k + … + n₁·p + n₀. Then the binomial coefficient C(m, n) leaves the same remainder on division by p as the product of the C(mᵢ, nᵢ) for i = 0, …, k, where C(a, b) is taken to be 0 when a < b.
nodes.by: Édouard Lucas, 1878
nodes.note: It gives the remainder of a binomial coefficient on division by a prime in terms of the base p digits of m and n. One consequence is that C(m, n) is divisible by p exactly when some base p digit of n is larger than the corresponding digit of m.

nodes.name: Zeckendorf's theorem
nodes.statement: Every positive integer can be written in exactly one way as a sum of one or more distinct Fibonacci numbers in which no two consecutive Fibonacci numbers appear.
nodes.by: Named after the amateur mathematician Edouard Zeckendorf
nodes.note: Such a sum is called the Zeckendorf representation of the number, and it can be found by a greedy algorithm that picks the largest possible Fibonacci number at each step.

nodes.name: Dirichlet's unit theorem
nodes.statement: For a number field K, the group of units of its ring of algebraic integers is finitely generated and has rank r₁ + r₂ − 1. Here r₁ is the number of real embeddings of K and r₂ is the number of pairs of complex-conjugate embeddings.
nodes.by: Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet
nodes.note: The rank is 1 for a real quadratic field and 0 for an imaginary quadratic field. The theory for real quadratic fields is essentially the theory of Pell's equation.

nodes.name: Dirichlet's approximation theorem
nodes.statement: For any real numbers α and N with N ≥ 1, there exist integers p and q with 1 ≤ q ≤ N such that |qα − p| ≤ 1/(⌊N⌋ + 1) < 1/N, where ⌊N⌋ is the integer part of N.
nodes.by: Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet
nodes.note: It follows that for any irrational α, the inequality |α − p/q| < 1/q² has infinitely many integer solutions p and q. The usual proof uses the pigeonhole principle.

nodes.name: Erdős–Delange theorem
nodes.statement: Let ω(n) be the number of prime factors of an integer n, counted with multiplicity, and let λ be any irrational number. Then the fractional parts of the numbers λω(n) are asymptotically uniformly distributed.
nodes.by: Stated without proof by Paul Erdős, 1946; Hubert Delange published a simpler proof, 1958
nodes.note: It implies the prime number theorem.

nodes.name: Chen's theorem
nodes.statement: Every sufficiently large even number can be written as the sum of two primes, or of a prime and a semiprime (a product of two primes).
nodes.by: Chen Jingrun, first stated 1966, with further details of the proof in 1973
nodes.note: It is a weakened form of Goldbach's conjecture, which states that every even number is the sum of two primes.

nodes.name: Deshouillers–Dress–Tenenbaum theorem
nodes.statement: Pick a divisor d of a natural number n uniformly at random and let D_n = log d / log n. Then for x ≥ 2 and uniformly for all t in [0, 1], the average (1/x) ∑_{n ≤ x} P(D_n ≤ t) equals (2/π) arcsin √t + O(1/√(log x)).
nodes.by: Jean-Marc Deshouillers, François Dress and Gérald Tenenbaum, 1979
nodes.note: The averaged distribution of D_n tends to the arcsine distribution, so very small and very large divisors are the most likely. Gintautas Bareikis and Eugenijus Manstavičius generalized it in 2007, with a beta distribution as the limit.

nodes.name: Divergence of the sum of the reciprocals of the primes
nodes.statement: The sum of the reciprocals of all prime numbers diverges: 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/5 + 1/7 + 1/11 + ... is infinite.
nodes.by: Leonhard Euler, 1737
nodes.note: It strengthens Euclid's result that there are infinitely many primes. The divergence is very slow, since the partial sums grow like log log n.

nodes.name: Grosswald–Schnitzer theorem
nodes.statement: Let pₙ be the n-th prime and choose real numbers qₙ with pₙ ≤ qₙ ≤ pₙ₊₁ for every n. Then ζ*(s) = ∏ 1/(1 − qₙ^(−s)) is nonzero for Re(s) > 1, extends to a meromorphic function on Re(s) > 0 with a simple pole at s = 1 whose residue r satisfies 1/2 ≤ r ≤ 1, and has exactly the same zeros, with the same multiplicities, as the Riemann zeta function ζ(s) in Re(s) > 0.
nodes.by: Emil Grosswald and Franz Josef Schnitzer, 1978
nodes.note: The zeros of the Riemann zeta function in Re(s) > 0 are therefore not tied to the primes alone. Grosswald and Schnitzer also proved a version for Dirichlet L-functions.

nodes.name: Centered polygonal number theorem
nodes.statement: Every positive integer is a sum of at most n + 2 centered n-gonal numbers.
nodes.by: Benjamin Lee Warren and Miroslav Kureš, 2025, generalizing the case of centered nonagonal numbers, which Frederick Pollock conjectured in 1850 and Kureš confirmed in 2023
nodes.note: For centered nonagonal numbers it says every positive integer is the sum of at most 11 of them.

nodes.name: Kronecker–Weber theorem
nodes.statement: Every finite abelian extension of the rational numbers ℚ is a subfield of a cyclotomic field. That is, any algebraic number field whose Galois group over ℚ is abelian lies inside a field obtained by adjoining a root of unity to ℚ.
nodes.by: First stated by Leopold Kronecker, 1853, with an argument incomplete for extensions of degree a power of 2; first complete proof by Hilbert, 1896
nodes.note: It is a partial converse to the fact that every cyclotomic field is an abelian extension of ℚ.

nodes.name: Rogers sieving theorem
nodes.statement: Exclude one arithmetic progression a_i + k·d_i for each of the differences d_1, …, d_n, and let m be the least common multiple of the d_i; then the number of residue classes modulo m that are not excluded is at most the number left when every offset a_i is 0, that is, when the excluded classes are t ≡ 0 (mod d_i). Equivalently, the natural density of the union of the progressions is smallest when all the offsets are 0.
nodes.by: C. A. Rogers, 1960s; in a modified form by Heini Halberstam and Klaus Roth in their 1966 book Sequences
nodes.note: For many years it was a folk theorem not well documented in the published literature. Its value as a principle in contemporary sieve theory was recognised after more than half a century.

nodes.name: Hensel's lemma
nodes.statement: Let h be a polynomial with integer coefficients whose leading coefficient a is not divisible by the prime p, and suppose h ≡ a·f·g modulo p, where f and g are monic polynomials (leading coefficient 1) that are coprime modulo p. Then for every positive integer k there are monic polynomials fₖ ≡ f and gₖ ≡ g modulo p with h ≡ a·fₖ·gₖ modulo pᵏ, unique modulo pᵏ; in particular a simple root of h modulo p lifts to a unique simple root modulo pᵏ that agrees with it modulo p.
nodes.by: Named after Kurt Hensel
nodes.note: Passing to the limit, a root or factorization modulo p lifts to one over the p-adic integers. The same proof works over any commutative ring with p replaced by a maximal ideal, and it gives an efficient algorithm used for factoring polynomials.

nodes.name: Lander, Parkin, and Selfridge conjecture
nodes.statement: Let k ≥ 2. If a sum of m positive integer k-th powers equals a sum of n positive integer k-th powers, and no number appears on both sides, then m + n ≥ k.
nodes.by: Posed by Leon J. Lander, Thomas R. Parkin and John Selfridge in their 1967 survey
nodes.note: For a single k-th power on one side it says that a sum of r k-th powers equal to a k-th power needs r ≥ k − 1, one less than Euler's sum of powers conjecture asserted.

nodes.name: Andrica's conjecture
nodes.statement: For every n, the square roots of the n-th prime p(n) and the next prime p(n+1) differ by less than 1: √p(n+1) − √p(n) < 1. Equivalently, the gap g(n) = p(n+1) − p(n) between consecutive primes always satisfies g(n) < 2√p(n) + 1.
nodes.note: Tables of maximal prime gaps confirm it exhaustively beyond 2⁶⁴. The difference √p(n+1) − √p(n) reaches its largest known value, about 0.670873, at n = 4.

nodes.name: Heegner's lemma
nodes.statement: Let y² = a₄x⁴ + a₃x³ + a₂x² + a₁x + a₀ be a curve over a field, where a₄ is not a square in that field. If the curve has a solution in some extension of the field of odd degree, then it has a solution in the field itself.
nodes.by: Kurt Heegner
nodes.note: Kurt Heegner used it in his paper on the class number problem.

nodes.name: Lindemann–Weierstrass theorem
nodes.statement: If α₁, …, αₙ are algebraic numbers that are linearly independent over the rational numbers, then e^α₁, …, e^αₙ are algebraically independent over ℚ; in other words, the field ℚ(e^α₁, …, e^αₙ) has transcendence degree n over ℚ. Equivalently, if α₁, …, αₙ are distinct algebraic numbers, then e^α₁, …, e^αₙ are linearly independent over the algebraic numbers.
nodes.by: Ferdinand von Lindemann proved in 1882 that e^α is transcendental for every non-zero algebraic α; Karl Weierstrass proved the general statement in 1885. Charles Hermite first proved the case where the exponents are rational integers.
nodes.note: The transcendence of e and π follows directly from it. It is extended by Baker's theorem, and Schanuel's conjecture would generalize it further.

nodes.name: Lochs's theorem
nodes.statement: For almost all real numbers in the interval (0,1), the ratio m/n tends to 6 ln(2) ln(10)/π² ≈ 0.97027014 as n grows, where m is the number of continued fraction terms needed to determine the first n decimal places of the number.
nodes.by: Gustav Lochs, proof published 1964
nodes.note: Since the limit is slightly below 1, each extra continued fraction term of a typical number adds about one decimal place of accuracy.

nodes.name: Barban–Davenport–Halberstam theorem
nodes.statement: For a coprime to q, let θ(x;q,a) be the sum of log p over all primes p ≤ x with p ≡ a mod q, and let E(x;q,a) = θ(x;q,a) − x/φ(q), where φ is Euler's totient function. Let V(x,Q) be the sum of |E(x;q,a)|² over all q ≤ Q and all a mod q coprime to q. Then V(x,Q) = O(Qx log x) + O(x²(log x)^(−A)) for 1 ≤ Q ≤ x and every positive A.
nodes.by: Barban and, separately, Davenport and Halberstam proved versions valid for Q ≤ x(log x)^(−B); this form is due to Gallagher
nodes.note: It estimates the error term in how evenly the primes are spread across arithmetic progressions with the same difference.

nodes.name: Mahler's 3/2 problem
nodes.statement: There are no Z-numbers. A Z-number is a positive real number x such that the fractional part of x·(3/2)ⁿ is less than 1/2 for every positive integer n.
nodes.by: Kurt Mahler, 1968
nodes.note: The conjecture would follow if Ω(3/2) exceeds 1/2. Flatto, Lagarias and Pollington showed that Ω(p/q) > 1/p for rational p/q > 1 in lowest terms.

nodes.name: Legendre's three-square theorem
nodes.statement: A natural number n can be written as a sum of three squares of integers, n = x² + y² + z², if and only if n is not of the form 4ᵃ(8b + 7) for nonnegative integers a and b.
nodes.by: First proved by A.-M. Legendre in 1797 or 1798; Gauss obtained a more general result in 1801
nodes.note: The first numbers that cannot be written as a sum of three squares are 7, 15, 23, 28, 31, 39, 47, 55, 60, 63, 71. The theorem can be used to prove Lagrange's four-square theorem.

nodes.name: Hurwitz's theorem
nodes.statement: For every irrational number ξ there are infinitely many pairs of relatively prime integers m, n such that |ξ − m/n| < 1/(√5·n²). The constant √5 cannot be replaced by any larger number.
nodes.by: Adolf Hurwitz, 1891
nodes.note: The condition that ξ is irrational cannot be omitted. The golden ratio (1+√5)/2 shows that the constant √5 is the best possible.

nodes.name: Fueter–Pólya theorem
nodes.statement: Let ℕ = {0, 1, 2, …}. If P is a real quadratic polynomial in two variables whose restriction to ℕ² is a bijection from ℕ² to ℕ, then P(x, y) = ½((x+y)² + 3x + y) or P(x, y) = ½((x+y)² + 3y + x).
nodes.by: First proved by Rudolf Fueter and George Pólya
nodes.note: Fueter proved it assuming P(0,0) = 0, and Pólya showed that this condition is not needed. M. A. Vsemirnov published an elementary proof in 2002.

nodes.name: Vinogradov's theorem
nodes.statement: For every positive real number A, r(N) = ½·G(N)·N² + O(N²/(log N)^A). Here r(N) is the sum of Λ(k₁)Λ(k₂)Λ(k₃) over all k₁ + k₂ + k₃ = N, Λ is the von Mangoldt function, and G(N) is the product over primes p dividing N of (1 − 1/(p−1)²) times the product over primes p not dividing N of (1 + 1/(p−1)³). As a consequence, every sufficiently large odd integer is a sum of three primes.
nodes.by: Ivan Matveyevich Vinogradov, 1937; Hardy and Littlewood had shown in 1923 that the result follows from the generalized Riemann hypothesis
nodes.note: It is a weaker form of Goldbach's weak conjecture, which would give such a representation for all odd integers greater than five. The proof uses the Hardy–Littlewood circle method.

nodes.name: Shintani's unit theorem
nodes.statement: For a number field, every subgroup of finite index of the totally positive units has a fundamental domain given by a rational polyhedric cone in the Minkowski space of the field.
nodes.by: Introduced by Shintani, 1976
nodes.note: It is a refinement of Dirichlet's unit theorem.

nodes.name: Davenport–Schmidt theorem
nodes.statement: Let ξ be a real number that is neither rational nor a quadratic irrational. Then there are infinitely many real numbers α that are rational or quadratic irrationals and satisfy |ξ − α| < C·H(α)^(−3)·max(1, ξ²), where C is any real number greater than 160/9 and H(α) is the largest absolute value among the coprime integers x, y, z, not all zero and with the first non-zero one positive, such that xα² + yα + z = 0.
nodes.by: Named after Harold Davenport and Wolfgang M. Schmidt
nodes.note: The theorem is related to Roth's theorem. It is effective: the constant C can be worked out for any given ξ.

nodes.name: Gillies' conjecture
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime and M_p = 2^p − 1. If A < B < √M_p, then as B/A and M_p tend to infinity, the number of prime divisors of M_p in the interval [A, B] is Poisson distributed with expected value log(log B / log A) if A ≥ 2p, and log(log B / log 2p) if A < 2p.
nodes.by: Donald B. Gillies, 1964
nodes.note: The conjecture implies that the number of Mersenne primes less than x is asymptotically 2 log log x / log 2. It disagrees with the Lenstra–Pomerance–Wagstaff conjecture, which is also open.

nodes.name: Ihara's lemma
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime that does not divide N, and let J_0(N) be the Jacobian of the compactification of the modular curve of Γ_0(N). Then the kernel of the sum of the two p-degeneracy maps from J_0(N) × J_0(N) to J_0(Np) is Eisenstein.
nodes.by: Introduced by Ihara and named by Ribet

nodes.name: Manin conjecture
nodes.statement: Let V be a Fano variety over a number field K, let H be a height function relative to the anticanonical divisor, and assume V(K) is Zariski dense in V. Then there is a non-empty Zariski open subset U of V such that the number N(B) of K-rational points x in U(K) with H(x) ≤ B satisfies N(B) ~ c·B·(log B)^(ρ−1) as B → ∞, where ρ is the rank of the Picard group of V and c is a positive constant.
nodes.by: Yuri I. Manin and his collaborators, 1989
nodes.note: It has been proved for special families of varieties. The constant c later received a conjectural interpretation by Peyre.

nodes.name: Jurkat–Richert theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a finite sequence of integers and P a set of primes. Let ω be a multiplicative function with ω(p)/p about the proportion of items of A divisible by p, let X approximate |A|, and let r_A(d) = |A_d| − (ω(d)/d)X, where A_d counts the items of A divisible by d. Suppose the sieve has dimension 1: there is a constant C with ∏_{z≤p<w} (1 − ω(p)/p)⁻¹ ≤ (log w / log z)(1 + C/log z) whenever 2 ≤ z < w. Then for all y and z with 2 ≤ z ≤ y ≤ X, the number S(A,P,z) of items of A that are coprime to the product P(z) of the primes of P below z satisfies XV(z)(f₁(s) − O(E)) − R ≤ S(A,P,z) ≤ XV(z)(F₁(s) + O(E)) + R. Here s = log y / log z, E = (log log y)^(3/4) / (log y)^(1/4), V(z) = ∏_{p∈P, p<z} (1 − ω(p)/p), R = ∑_{m | P(z), m < y} 4^ν(m) |r_A(m)| with ν(m) the number of distinct prime divisors of m, and F₁ and f₁ are fixed functions defined by difference differential equations.
nodes.by: Wolfgang B. Jurkat and Hans-Egon Richert, 1965
nodes.note: It is a key ingredient in proofs of Chen's theorem on Goldbach's conjecture. The book of Diamond and Halberstam extends the theorem to sieve dimensions higher than 1.

nodes.name: Kaplansky's theorem on quadratic forms
nodes.statement: A prime p congruent to 1 modulo 16 is representable by both or by neither of x² + 32y² and x² + 64y². A prime p congruent to 9 modulo 16 is representable by exactly one of these two forms.
nodes.by: Irving Kaplansky, 2003
nodes.note: The primes represented by each of these forms individually are not describable by congruence conditions.

nodes.name: Neukirch–Uchida theorem
nodes.statement: Let K₁ and K₂ be algebraic number fields. Every isomorphism φ of topological groups between their absolute Galois groups (with the Krull topology) comes from a unique field isomorphism σ between their algebraic closures with σ(K₁) = K₂ and φ(g) = σ∘g∘σ⁻¹ for every g. In particular, K₁ and K₂ are isomorphic exactly when their absolute Galois groups are isomorphic as topological groups.
nodes.by: Jürgen Neukirch, who showed that number fields with the same absolute Galois group are isomorphic, and Kôji Uchida, who proved Neukirch's stronger conjecture
nodes.note: It is one of the foundational results of anabelian geometry. Florian Pop extended the result to infinite fields that are finitely generated over prime fields.

nodes.name: Wolstenholme's theorem
nodes.statement: For every prime number p ≥ 5, the binomial coefficient C(2p − 1, p − 1) is congruent to 1 modulo p³.
nodes.by: Joseph Wolstenholme, 1862; Charles Babbage showed the same congruence modulo p² in 1819
nodes.note: For p = 7 it says that 1716 is one more than a multiple of 343. It can also be expressed as a pair of congruences for harmonic numbers.

nodes.name: Euclidean division theorem
nodes.statement: For any integers a and b with b ≠ 0, there exist unique integers q and r such that a = bq + r and 0 ≤ r < |b|.
nodes.note: The integers a, b, q and r are called the dividend, divisor, quotient and remainder. The theorem is often called the division algorithm, although it is a theorem and not an algorithm.

nodes.name: Euclid–Euler theorem
nodes.statement: An even natural number is perfect, meaning it equals the sum of its divisors smaller than itself, if and only if it equals 2^(p−1)(2^p − 1) for some p such that 2^p − 1 is a prime number.
nodes.by: Euclid proved the "if" part; Alhazen conjectured the "only if" part around 1000 CE; Leonhard Euler proved it in the 18th century
nodes.note: It gives a one-to-one correspondence between even perfect numbers and Mersenne primes. It is unknown whether any odd perfect number exists.

nodes.name: Vinogradov's mean value theorem
nodes.statement: Let s and k be positive integers and let J_{s,k}(X) be the number of solutions in whole numbers 1 ≤ xᵢ, yᵢ ≤ X of the k equations x₁ʲ + … + x_sʲ = y₁ʲ + … + y_sʲ for j = 1, 2, …, k. Then for every ε > 0 there is a constant C, depending on s, k and ε but not on X, such that J_{s,k}(X) ≤ C(X^(s+ε) + X^(2s − k(k+1)/2 + ε)).
nodes.by: Named after I. M. Vinogradov, whose original weaker theorem dates from 1935; the main conjecture was proved by Jean Bourgain, Ciprian Demeter and Larry Guth, and by a different method by Trevor Wooley
nodes.note: A strong bound on J_{s,k}(X) is an important part of the Hardy–Littlewood method for Waring's problem and of proofs of a zero-free region for the Riemann zeta function. The lower bound J_{s,k}(X) ≫ X^s + X^(2s − k(k+1)/2) shows that the estimate is nearly optimal.

nodes.name: First Hardy–Littlewood conjecture
nodes.statement: Let m₁, …, m_k be positive even integers such that the numbers p, p+m₁, …, p+m_k do not form a complete residue system modulo any prime. Then the number of primes p < n for which p+m₁, …, p+m_k are all prime is asymptotic to C·∫₂ⁿ dt/(log t)^(k+1), where C = 2^k times the product over odd primes q of (1 − w(q)/q)/(1 − 1/q)^(k+1), and w(q) is the number of distinct residues of 0, m₁, …, m_k modulo q.
nodes.by: G. H. Hardy and J. E. Littlewood, 1923
nodes.note: The case k = 1, m₁ = 2 is related to the twin prime conjecture and involves the twin prime constant. The Bateman–Horn conjecture generalizes it to polynomials of higher degree.

nodes.name: Fermat's right triangle theorem
nodes.statement: A right triangle in the Euclidean plane whose three side lengths are all rational numbers cannot have an area that is the square of a rational number.
nodes.by: Published in 1670 among the works of Pierre de Fermat, soon after his death; it is the only complete proof given by Fermat. One equivalent formulation was stated, but not proved, by Fibonacci in 1225
nodes.note: The area of a rational-sided right triangle is called a congruent number, so no congruent number can be square. An immediate consequence is that Fermat's Last Theorem is true for exponent 4.

nodes.name: Fermat's little theorem
nodes.statement: If p is a prime number, then for any integer a, a^p − a is an integer multiple of p, that is, a^p ≡ a (mod p). If a is not divisible by p, this is equivalent to a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p).
nodes.by: Stated by Pierre de Fermat, 1640; first published proof by Euler, 1736
nodes.note: It is the basis for the Fermat primality test. It is called the little theorem to distinguish it from Fermat's Last Theorem.

nodes.name: Ramanujan–Nagell equation
nodes.statement: The equation 2ⁿ − 7 = x² has solutions in natural numbers n and x only for n = 3, 4, 5, 7 and 15, which give x = 1, 3, 5, 11 and 181.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Srinivasa Ramanujan, 1913; proposed independently by Wilhelm Ljunggren, 1943; proved by Trygve Nagell, 1948
nodes.note: It is an exponential Diophantine equation. It implies that there are no perfect binary codes with minimum Hamming distance 5 or 6.

nodes.name: Hasse–Minkowski theorem
nodes.statement: Two quadratic forms over a number field are equivalent if and only if they are equivalent over every completion of the field (real, complex or p-adic). Also, a quadratic form over a number field nontrivially represents zero if and only if it does so over every completion.
nodes.by: Proved for the rational numbers by Hermann Minkowski and generalized to number fields by Helmut Hasse
nodes.note: The same statement holds for all global fields. It is the first significant example of a local-global principle.

nodes.name: Chinese remainder theorem
nodes.statement: Let n₁, …, n_k be integers greater than 1 that are pairwise coprime (no two share a common factor other than 1), and let N be their product. Then for any integers a₁, …, a_k with 0 ≤ a_i < n_i for every i, there is exactly one integer x with 0 ≤ x < N whose remainder on division by each n_i is a_i.
nodes.by: Earliest known statement, as a single example, in the Sunzi Suanjing by Sunzi (3rd to 5th century); algorithm by Aryabhata (6th century); complete solution (Da-yan-shu) by Qin Jiushao, 1247
nodes.note: It is widely used for computing with large integers, because one computation can be replaced by several similar computations on small integers. In terms of congruences it holds over every principal ideal domain.

nodes.name: Euler's theorem
nodes.statement: If n and a are coprime positive integers, then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n), where φ is Euler's totient function. Conversely, if this congruence holds, then a and n are coprime.
nodes.by: Leonhard Euler: proof of Fermat's little theorem (the case of prime n), 1736; generalization to non-prime n, 1763
nodes.note: It underlies the RSA cryptosystem and is used to reduce large powers modulo n.

nodes.name: Siegel's lemma
nodes.statement: Take a system of M linear equations in N unknowns with N > M, set equal to 0, whose coefficients are integers, not all 0, of absolute value at most B. Then the system has a solution in integers X₁, …, X_N, not all 0, each of absolute value at most (NB)^(M/(N−M)).
nodes.by: Carl Ludwig Siegel, 1929; the existence of the auxiliary polynomials was proven by Axel Thue; Bombieri and Vaaler gave a sharper bound in 1983
nodes.note: It is a pure existence theorem for a system of linear equations. Thue's proof used the pigeonhole principle, and Bombieri and Vaaler replaced it by techniques from the geometry of numbers.

nodes.name: Euclid's lemma
nodes.statement: If a prime number p divides a product ab of two integers, then p divides a or p divides b (or both).
nodes.by: Euclid, in the Elements (Book VII, Proposition 30)
nodes.note: The statement can fail when p is composite: 10 divides 4 × 15 = 60 but divides neither 4 nor 15. It is the key step in the proof of the fundamental theorem of arithmetic and is used to define prime elements in commutative rings.

nodes.name: Gauss circle problem
nodes.statement: Let N(r) be the number of pairs of integers (m, n) with m² + n² ≤ r², and let E(r) = N(r) − πr². Then for every ε > 0 there is a constant C such that |E(r)| ≤ C·r^(1/2+ε) for all sufficiently large r.
nodes.by: Named after Carl Friedrich Gauss, who made the first progress
nodes.note: Hardy and Landau showed in 1915 that |E(r)| is not o(r^(1/2)(log r)^(1/4)). The best proven upper exponent is 131/208, by Martin Huxley in 2000.

nodes.name: Nicomachus's theorem
nodes.statement: For every positive integer n, the sum of the first n cubes equals the square of the nth triangular number: 1³ + 2³ + 3³ + ⋯ + n³ = (1 + 2 + 3 + ⋯ + n)².
nodes.by: Named after Nicomachus of Gerasa, c. 60
nodes.note: Nicomachus observed that the first odd number is 1³, the sum of the next two is 2³, the sum of the next three is 3³, and so on, and the identity follows from this. It also appears in the works of Aryabhata in the 5th century and Al-Karaji around 1000.

nodes.name: Vantieghem's theorem
nodes.statement: A natural number n ≥ 3 is prime if and only if the product (2¹ − 1)(2² − 1)⋯(2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1) leaves remainder n when divided by 2ⁿ − 1.
nodes.note: It is a primality criterion. Equivalent versions hold as congruences of polynomials in X.

nodes.name: Agoh–Giuga conjecture
nodes.statement: An integer p greater than 1 is prime if and only if p·Bₚ₋₁ ≡ −1 (mod p), where Bₖ denotes the Bernoulli numbers.
nodes.by: Takashi Agoh; an equivalent formulation was given by Giuseppe Giuga, 1950
nodes.note: Giuga's equivalent form says that p is prime if and only if 1ᵖ⁻¹ + 2ᵖ⁻¹ + ⋯ + (p−1)ᵖ⁻¹ ≡ −1 (mod p), and for prime p this follows from Fermat's little theorem. A composite number satisfies the congruence only if it is both a Carmichael number and a Giuga number, and such a number would have at least 13,800 digits.

nodes.name: Legendre's formula
nodes.statement: For any prime p and any positive integer n, the exponent of the largest power of p that divides n! equals the sum over i ≥ 1 of ⌊n/pⁱ⌋. Only finitely many terms are nonzero, since ⌊n/pⁱ⌋ = 0 once pⁱ > n.
nodes.by: Named after Adrien-Marie Legendre; also known as de Polignac's formula, after Alphonse de Polignac
nodes.note: Equivalently, the exponent equals (n − s(n))/(p − 1), where s(n) is the sum of the digits of n in base p. The formula can be used to prove Kummer's theorem.

nodes.name: Euler's criterion
nodes.statement: Let p be an odd prime and a an integer coprime to p. Then a^((p−1)/2) ≡ 1 (mod p) if there is an integer x with x² ≡ a (mod p), and a^((p−1)/2) ≡ −1 (mod p) if there is no such integer.
nodes.by: Leonhard Euler, 1748
nodes.note: It gives a formula for deciding whether an integer is a quadratic residue modulo a prime. Equivalently, the Legendre symbol (a/p) is congruent to a^((p−1)/2) mod p.

nodes.name: Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem
nodes.statement: Let K be a field of characteristic zero, such as the complex numbers. Let u₁, u₂, … be a sequence in K in which every term from some point on equals the same fixed linear combination, with coefficients in K, of the d terms before it. Then the set of positions n at which uₙ = 0 is the union of finitely many arithmetic progressions and a finite set.
nodes.by: Thoralf Skolem proved it for sequences of rational numbers, Kurt Mahler for sequences of algebraic numbers, and Christer Lech for sequences with values in any field of characteristic zero
nodes.note: The known proofs use p-adic analysis and are non-constructive.

nodes.name: Well-ordering principle
nodes.statement: Every non-empty set of nonnegative integers contains a least element.
nodes.note: Depending on how the natural numbers are introduced, this property is either an axiom or a provable theorem; in Peano arithmetic it is derived from the principle of mathematical induction. It justifies proofs that assume a counterexample exists and then take a smallest one.

nodes.name: Gauss's lemma
nodes.statement: Let p be an odd prime and a an integer coprime to p. Take the numbers a, 2a, 3a, …, ((p−1)/2)a and their least positive residues modulo p, and let n be the number of these residues that are greater than p/2. Then the Legendre symbol (a/p) equals (−1)ⁿ.
nodes.by: Carl Friedrich Gauss, 1808; proved again by him in 1818
nodes.note: It gives a condition for an integer to be a quadratic residue and is involved in some proofs of quadratic reciprocity.

nodes.name: Thaine's theorem
nodes.statement: Let p and q be distinct odd primes with q not dividing p−1. Let F = ℚ(ζ_p⁺), let G⁺ be the Galois group of F over ℚ, E the group of units of F, C its subgroup of cyclotomic units, and Cl⁺ the class group of F. If an element θ of the group ring ℤ[G⁺] annihilates E/CE^q, then θ annihilates Cl⁺/(Cl⁺)^q.
nodes.by: Francisco Thaine, 1988
nodes.note: It is an analogue of Stickelberger's theorem for real abelian fields. Thaine's method has been used to shorten the proof of the Mazur–Wiles theorem and in the proof of Mihăilescu's theorem.

nodes.name: n conjecture
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 3 and let a₁, …, aₙ be integers with gcd 1, sum 0, and no proper subsum equal to 0. Then for every ε > 0 there is a constant C depending on n and ε such that the largest of |a₁|, …, |aₙ| is less than C times rad(|a₁|·…·|aₙ|) to the power 2n − 5 + ε, where rad(m) is the product of the distinct prime factors of m.
nodes.by: Browkin and Brzeziński, 1994
nodes.note: It generalizes the abc conjecture to more than three integers.

nodes.name: Schinzel's theorem
nodes.statement: For every positive integer n there is a circle in the plane that passes through exactly n points with integer coordinates.
nodes.by: Andrzej Schinzel
nodes.note: For even n = 2k the circle (x − 1/2)² + y² = 5^(k−1)/4 works, and for odd n = 2k + 1 the circle (x − 1/3)² + y² = 5^(2k)/9. These circles are not the smallest possible, but they have explicit equations.

nodes.name: Hilbert's seventh problem
nodes.statement: If a is an algebraic number other than 0 and 1, and b is an irrational algebraic number, then aᵇ is transcendental. An algebraic number is a root of a non-zero polynomial with rational coefficients, and a transcendental number is a number that is not algebraic.
nodes.by: Posed by David Hilbert, 1900; proved independently by Aleksandr Gelfond and Theodor Schneider, 1934
nodes.note: Kuzmin proved the case where b is a real quadratic irrational in 1930, which shows that 2^√2 is transcendental. The general result is known as the Gelfond–Schneider theorem.

nodes.name: Wilson's theorem
nodes.statement: A natural number n > 1 is prime if and only if (n − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod n). Equivalently, n > 1 is prime exactly when n divides (n − 1)! + 1.
nodes.by: First stated by Ibn al-Haytham, c. 1000 AD; announced by Edward Waring in 1770 without proof, crediting John Wilson; first proved by Lagrange, 1771
nodes.note: In practice it is useless as a primality test, because computing (n − 1)! modulo n for large n is computationally complex. Gauss generalized it to the product of the positive integers below m that are coprime to m.

nodes.name: Stark–Heegner theorem
nodes.statement: For a square-free integer d < 0, the quadratic field ℚ(√d) has class number one, equivalently its ring of integers is a principal ideal domain, if and only if d is one of −1, −2, −3, −7, −11, −19, −43, −67, −163.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Gauss, 1798; essentially proven by Kurt Heegner, 1952, but not accepted until Harold Stark published a proof in 1967; Alan Baker gave a slightly earlier proof in 1966 by different methods
nodes.note: It solves a special case of Gauss's class number problem. The listed values of d are known as the Heegner numbers.

nodes.name: Ostrowski's theorem
nodes.statement: Every non-trivial absolute value on the rational numbers is equivalent to either the usual real absolute value or a p-adic absolute value for some prime p. Two absolute values are equivalent if they induce the same topology.
nodes.by: Alexander Ostrowski, 1916
nodes.note: An absolute value on ℚ is a function that is non-negative, zero only at 0, multiplicative, and satisfies the triangle inequality.

nodes.name: Second Hardy–Littlewood conjecture
nodes.statement: For all integers x and y that are at least 2, the number of primes up to x + y is at most the number of primes up to x plus the number of primes up to y. In symbols, π(x + y) ≤ π(x) + π(y).
nodes.by: G. H. Hardy and John Edensor Littlewood, 1923
nodes.note: It was proposed together with the first Hardy–Littlewood conjecture on prime k-tuples, and the two have been proved inconsistent with each other. If the first conjecture holds, the first counterexample is expected for x between 1.5 × 10¹⁷⁴ and 2.2 × 10¹¹⁹⁸.

nodes.name: Erdős–Turán conjecture on additive bases
nodes.statement: Let B be a set of natural numbers and let r_B(n) be the number of pairs (a₁, a₂) of elements of B with a₁ + a₂ = n. If r_B(n) > 0 for all sufficiently large n, then r_B(n) is not bounded: its limit superior as n tends to infinity is infinite.
nodes.by: Paul Erdős and Pál Turán, 1941
nodes.note: Roughly, it says that the number of ways of writing a number as a sum of two elements of an additive basis cannot stay bounded. In 2006 Borwein, Choi and Chu proved that this number eventually exceeds 7.

nodes.name: Dickson's conjecture
nodes.statement: Let a₁ + b₁n, a₂ + b₂n, …, a_k + b_kn be finitely many linear forms with integer coefficients and each b_i ≥ 1. Unless a congruence condition prevents it, meaning that some prime p divides at least one of the forms for every n, there are infinitely many positive integers n for which all k forms are prime.
nodes.by: Leonard Dickson, 1903
nodes.note: The case k = 1 is Dirichlet's theorem. Two other special cases are the conjectures that there are infinitely many twin primes and infinitely many Sophie Germain primes.

nodes.name: Grimm's conjecture
nodes.statement: If n + 1, n + 2, …, n + k are all composite numbers, then there are k distinct prime numbers p₁, …, p_k such that each p_i divides n + i for 1 ≤ i ≤ k.
nodes.by: Carl Albert Grimm, 1969
nodes.note: The conjecture has been verified for all n < 1.9×10¹⁰.

nodes.name: Leopoldt's conjecture
nodes.statement: For a number field K and a prime p, the p-adic regulator of K does not vanish. Equivalently, if E₁ is the group of global units of K that are principal units at every prime of K above p, then the closure of E₁, embedded diagonally in the product of those groups of principal units, has ℤ_p-module rank r₁ + r₂ − 1, where r₁ is the number of real embeddings of K and r₂ the number of pairs of complex embeddings.
nodes.by: Introduced by Heinrich-Wolfgang Leopoldt
nodes.note: It is known when K is an abelian extension of the rationals or of an imaginary quadratic number field. The p-adic regulator is defined like the usual regulator but with p-adic logarithms.

nodes.name: Riemann–Siegel formula
nodes.statement: For non-negative integers M and N, the Riemann zeta function satisfies ζ(s) = ∑ₙ₌₁ᴺ n⁻ˢ + γ(1−s) ∑ₙ₌₁ᴹ nˢ⁻¹ + R(s), where γ(s) = π^(1/2−s) Γ(s/2)/Γ((1−s)/2) is the factor in the functional equation ζ(s) = γ(1−s) ζ(1−s). Here R(s) = −Γ(1−s)/(2πi) ∫ (−x)^(s−1) e^(−Nx)/(eˣ−1) dx, taken over a contour that starts and ends at +∞ and circles the singularities of absolute value at most 2πM.
nodes.by: Found by Siegel, 1932, in unpublished manuscripts of Bernhard Riemann dating from the 1850s
nodes.note: Siegel and Edwards apply the method of steepest descent to the integral R(s) to obtain an asymptotic expansion of the error term as a series of negative powers of Im(s). Gabcke (1979) found good bounds for the error of the formula.

nodes.name: First Kronecker limit formula
nodes.statement: For τ = x + iy with y > 0, let E(τ,s) = ∑ y^s / |mτ+n|^(2s), summed over all integer pairs (m,n) ≠ (0,0) for Re(s) > 1 and extended to other complex s by analytic continuation. Then E(τ,s) = π/(s−1) + 2π(γ − log 2 − log(√y |η(τ)|²)) + O(s−1), where γ is the Euler–Mascheroni constant and η is the Dedekind eta function.
nodes.by: Named for Leopold Kronecker
nodes.note: The Eisenstein series has a pole at s = 1 with residue π, and the formula gives the constant term of its Laurent series there.

nodes.name: Landsberg–Schaar relation
nodes.statement: For all positive integers p and q, (1/√p) times the sum over n = 0, …, p − 1 of exp(2πi n²q/p) equals (e^(πi/4)/√(2q)) times the sum over n = 0, …, 2q − 1 of exp(−πi n²p/(2q)).
nodes.note: The standard proof uses an identity of Jacobi, a special case of the Poisson summation formula, and a proof using only finite methods was found by Ben Moore in 2018. For q = 1 it reduces to a formula for the quadratic Gauss sum modulo p.

nodes.name: Zolotarev's lemma
nodes.statement: For an odd prime p and an integer a not divisible by p, the Legendre symbol (a/p) equals the sign of the permutation of the nonzero residue classes mod p given by multiplication by a.
nodes.by: Yegor Ivanovich Zolotarev, 1872
nodes.note: Zolotarev introduced it in a proof of quadratic reciprocity. It is equivalent to Gauss's lemma and extends to the Jacobi symbol.

nodes.name: Class number formula
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field with r₁ real embeddings and 2r₂ complex embeddings. Its Dedekind zeta function ζ_K(s) converges absolutely for Re(s) > 1 and extends to a meromorphic function on all complex s whose only pole is a simple pole at s = 1. The residue there is 2^r₁ · (2π)^r₂ · Reg_K · h_K / (w_K · √|D_K|), where h_K is the class number, Reg_K the regulator, w_K the number of roots of unity in K, and D_K the discriminant of K.
nodes.note: It relates invariants of a number field to a special value of its Dedekind zeta function. Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet published a proof of the formula for quadratic fields in 1839, stated in the language of quadratic forms, and Gauss appears to have known that case in 1801.

nodes.name: Hasse's theorem on elliptic curves
nodes.statement: If N is the number of points on an elliptic curve E over a finite field with q elements, then |N − (q+1)| ≤ 2√q.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Emil Artin in his thesis; proved by Helmut Hasse, 1933, with the proof published in 1936
nodes.note: It is equivalent to determining the absolute value of the roots of the local zeta-function of E, and is the analogue of the Riemann hypothesis for the function field of the curve.

nodes.name: Ax–Kochen theorem
nodes.statement: For each positive integer d there is a finite set Y_d of prime numbers such that, for every prime p not in Y_d, every homogeneous polynomial of degree d over the p-adic numbers in at least d² + 1 variables has a nontrivial zero.
nodes.by: Named after James Ax and Simon B. Kochen
nodes.note: Emil Artin conjectured that no exceptional primes are needed, but Guy Terjanian found a 2-adic counterexample of degree 4 in 18 variables. The proof compares p-adic fields with fields of formal Laurent series over finite fields, using ultraproducts and Serge Lang's theorem.

nodes.name: Erdős–Fuchs theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be an infinite set of natural numbers, and let s(x) be the number of ordered pairs (k₁, k₂) of elements of A with k₁ + k₂ ≤ x. Then there is no constant c > 0 for which s(n) = cn + o(n^(1/4) (log n)^(−1/2)) holds.
nodes.by: Paul Erdős and Wolfgang Heinrich Johannes Fuchs, 1956
nodes.note: It says that the average number of ways to write a number as a sum of two elements of a set cannot be too close to a linear function. It is stronger than a 1941 conjecture of Erdős and Turán that s(n) = cn + O(1) cannot hold.

nodes.name: Takagi existence theorem
nodes.statement: For any number field K there is an inclusion-reversing correspondence between the finite abelian extensions of K (inside a fixed algebraic closure of K) and the generalized ideal class groups defined via a modulus of K, under which each such group is the Galois group of its extension. The correspondence is one-to-one once generalized ideal class groups for different moduli that give the same extension are treated as equivalent.
nodes.by: Takagi, who proved it during World War I and presented it at the International Congress of Mathematicians in 1920; published in Mathematische Annalen in 1925
nodes.note: It is called an existence theorem because a main burden of the proof is to show the existence of enough abelian extensions of K. Its special case for the Hilbert class field was proved by Philipp Furtwängler in 1907.

nodes.name: Baker's theorem
nodes.statement: If logarithms log α₁, …, log αₙ of nonzero algebraic numbers are linearly independent over the rational numbers, then they are linearly independent over the algebraic numbers. Moreover, β₀ + β₁ log α₁ + ⋯ + βₙ log αₙ is never 0 when β₀, …, βₙ and α₁, …, αₙ are nonzero algebraic numbers, and Baker gave an effective lower bound for its absolute value.
nodes.by: Alan Baker, 1966; he removed an assumption about 2πi and gave the inhomogeneous version in 1967
nodes.note: It subsumes the Hermite–Lindemann and Gelfond–Schneider theorems. Baker used it to derive effective bounds for solutions of some Diophantine equations and to find all imaginary quadratic fields with class number 1.

nodes.name: Birch's theorem
nodes.statement: Let K be an algebraic number field, let k, l and n be natural numbers, and let f₁, …, f_k be homogeneous polynomials in n variables with coefficients in K, of odd degrees r₁, …, r_k. Then there is a number ψ(r₁, …, r_k, l, K) such that if n ≥ ψ(r₁, …, r_k, l, K), there is an l-dimensional vector subspace V of Kⁿ on which f₁ = … = f_k = 0.
nodes.by: Named after Bryan John Birch

nodes.name: Hilbert–Speiser theorem
nodes.statement: A finite abelian extension K of the rational numbers ℚ has a normal integral basis if and only if it is tamely ramified over ℚ.
nodes.by: Introduced by Hilbert in his Zahlbericht and by Speiser, 1916
nodes.note: Equivalently, K is a subfield of ℚ(ζₙ) where n is a squarefree odd number. A converse says that this property holds for all tamely ramified abelian extensions of a number field J only when J = ℚ.

nodes.name: Jacobi's four-square theorem
nodes.statement: The number of ways to write a positive integer n as a sum of four squares of integers, where different orders and different integers being squared (such as 1 and −1) count as different ways, is eight times the sum of the divisors of n if n is odd, and 24 times the sum of the odd divisors of n if n is even. Equivalently, it is eight times the sum of the divisors of n that are not divisible by 4.
nodes.by: Carl Gustav Jakob Jacobi, 1834
nodes.note: An immediate consequence is that 2n and 8n have the same number of such representations.

nodes.name: Sophie Germain's theorem
nodes.statement: Let p be an odd prime and suppose there is an auxiliary prime q such that no two nonzero p-th powers differ by one modulo q, and p is not a p-th power modulo q. Then in any solution of xᵖ + yᵖ = zᵖ in integers at least one of x, y, z is divisible by p², so the first case of Fermat's Last Theorem, where p does not divide xyz, holds for p.
nodes.by: Sophie Germain; attributed to her by Adrien-Marie Legendre, 1823
nodes.note: Germain found such an auxiliary prime for every prime p less than 100.

nodes.name: Stickelberger's theorem
nodes.statement: Let F be an abelian number field with Galois group G_F over ℚ and Stickelberger element θ(F). Then the Stickelberger ideal of F annihilates the class group of F: if α in ℤ[G_F] is such that αθ(F) = ∑ a_σ σ lies in ℤ[G_F], and J is any fractional ideal of F, then the product over σ in G_F of σ(J^{a_σ}) is a principal ideal.
nodes.by: Special case first proven by Ernst Kummer, 1847; general result by Ludwig Stickelberger, 1890
nodes.note: It gives information about the Galois module structure of class groups of cyclotomic fields. The element θ(F) itself need not annihilate the class group.

nodes.name: Principal ideal theorem
nodes.statement: For any algebraic number field K, let L be its Hilbert class field and O_L the ring of integers of L. Then every ideal I of the ring of integers of K becomes a principal ideal when extended to O_L, that is, I·O_L = α·O_L for some element α of O_L.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Hilbert, 1902; Artin reduced it to a question about finite groups; proved by Philipp Furtwängler, 1929
nodes.note: It was the last remaining part of Hilbert's program on class fields to be completed. The phenomenon is also called principalization or capitulation.

nodes.name: Hasse norm theorem
nodes.statement: Let L/K be a cyclic extension of number fields. If a nonzero element of K is a local norm everywhere, that is, a norm from the completion of L at every prime of K, archimedean and non-archimedean, then it is a global norm: the relative norm of some element of L.
nodes.by: Hasse, 1931; the case of degree 2 was proved by Hilbert, 1897, and the case of prime degree by Furtwangler, 1902
nodes.note: It is an example of a local-global principle. It is no longer true in general if the extension is abelian but not cyclic: Hasse showed that 3 is a local norm everywhere for ℚ(√−3, √13)/ℚ but not a global norm.

nodes.name: Von Staudt–Clausen theorem
nodes.statement: For every positive integer n, adding to the Bernoulli number B₂ₙ the sum of 1/p over all primes p for which p − 1 divides 2n gives an integer.
nodes.by: Found independently by von Staudt and Clausen, 1840
nodes.note: It determines the fractional part of Bernoulli numbers. As a consequence, the denominators of the nonzero Bernoulli numbers B₂ₙ are the products of all primes p for which p − 1 divides 2n, so they are square-free and divisible by 6.

nodes.name: Six exponentials theorem
nodes.statement: If x₁, x₂, x₃ are complex numbers linearly independent over the rational numbers, and y₁, y₂ are complex numbers linearly independent over the rational numbers, then at least one of the six numbers e^(x₁y₁), e^(x₁y₂), e^(x₂y₁), e^(x₂y₂), e^(x₃y₁), e^(x₃y₂) is transcendental.
