nodes.by: First explicitly stated and proved in complete form independently by Serge Lang and Kanakanahalli Ramachandra in the 1960s; a special case was mentioned by Alaoglu and Erdős in 1944
nodes.note: It follows from the stronger five exponentials theorem. The four exponentials conjecture, which would strengthen it further, is still unproven.

nodes.name: Three-gap theorem
nodes.statement: If n points are placed on a circle at angles θ, 2θ, 3θ, ..., nθ from a starting point, then there are at most three distinct distances between points in adjacent positions around the circle. Equivalently, for any positive real number α and positive integer n, the fractional parts of α, 2α, ..., nα divide the unit interval into subintervals of at most three different lengths.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Hugo Steinhaus; first proofs in the late 1950s by Vera T. Sós and Stanisław Świerczkowski
nodes.note: When there are three distances, the largest equals the sum of the other two. It is also known as the three-distance theorem or the Steinhaus conjecture.

nodes.name: Oppermann's conjecture
nodes.statement: For every integer n > 1, there is at least one prime number between n(n − 1) and n², and at least one more prime between n² and n(n + 1).
nodes.by: Ludvig Oppermann, announced in an unpublished lecture in March 1877
nodes.note: It is closely related to but stronger than Legendre's conjecture, Andrica's conjecture and Brocard's conjecture. If true, it would mean there are at least two primes between n² and (n + 1)².

nodes.name: Riemann–von Mangoldt formula
nodes.statement: The number N(T) of zeros of the Riemann zeta function with imaginary part greater than 0 and less than or equal to T satisfies N(T) = (T/2π)·log(T/2π) − T/2π + O(log T).
nodes.by: Stated by Bernhard Riemann, 1859; proved by Hans Carl Friedrich von Mangoldt, 1905
nodes.note: It describes the distribution of the zeros of the Riemann zeta function. Under the Lindelöf and Riemann hypotheses the error term can be improved.

nodes.name: Proth's theorem
nodes.statement: Let p = k·2ⁿ + 1, where k is a positive odd integer with k < 2ⁿ (a Proth number). If there is an integer a with a^((p−1)/2) ≡ −1 (mod p), then p is prime.
nodes.by: François Proth, 1878
nodes.note: It is the basis of Proth's primality test for Proth numbers. The converse also holds: if a Proth number p is prime, such an a exists.

nodes.name: Sophie Germain's identity
nodes.statement: For all x and y, x⁴ + 4y⁴ = ((x + y)² + y²)·((x − y)² + y²) = (x² + 2xy + 2y²)·(x² − 2xy + 2y²).
nodes.by: Named after Sophie Germain; the attribution to her was made by Leonard Eugene Dickson, and the identity does not appear in her works
nodes.note: It is used to factorize integers of the form x⁴ + 4y⁴ and often appears in competition problems. It shows, for example, that n⁴ + 4ⁿ is never prime for n > 1.

nodes.name: Herbrand–Ribet theorem
nodes.statement: Let p be an odd prime and let G be the p-primary part of the ideal class group of the field ℚ(ζ) of p-th roots of unity. Split G as a direct sum of pieces G_n (n = 1, …, p − 1) using the idempotents built from the Teichmüller character. Then for odd n, G_n is nontrivial if and only if p divides the Bernoulli number B_(p−n).
nodes.by: Jacques Herbrand (if G_n is nontrivial then p divides B_(p−n)); converse by Kenneth Ribet
nodes.note: It strengthens Ernst Kummer's theorem that p divides the class number of ℚ(ζ) if and only if p divides the numerator of some Bernoulli number B_n with 0 < n < p − 1. The main conjecture of Iwasawa theory, proved by Mazur and Wiles, sharpens it further.

nodes.name: Carmichael's theorem
nodes.statement: Let P and Q be relatively prime integers with PQ ≠ 0 and P² − 4Q > 0, and let U₀ = 0, U₁ = 1, Uₙ = P·Uₙ₋₁ − Q·Uₙ₋₂ be the Lucas sequence of the first kind. Then for every n other than 1, 2 and 6, Uₙ has a prime divisor that divides no earlier term, except for U₁₂(±1, −1) = ±144. In particular, for n greater than 12 the nth Fibonacci number has a prime divisor that divides no earlier Fibonacci number.
nodes.by: R. D. Carmichael, 1913; a simple proof by Yabuta, 2001
nodes.note: A prime dividing Uₙ but no earlier term is called a primitive prime divisor of Uₙ. In 2001 Bilu, Hanrot, Voutier and Mignotte extended the theorem to negative discriminants, where it holds for all n > 30.

nodes.name: Equidistribution theorem
nodes.statement: If a is an irrational number, the sequence a, 2a, 3a, ... taken mod 1 is uniformly distributed on the circle ℝ/ℤ. In the long run, every arc of the circle receives a share of the terms equal to its length.
nodes.by: Proved in 1909 and 1910 separately by Hermann Weyl, Wacław Sierpiński and Piers Bohl
nodes.note: It is a special case of the ergodic theorem, taking the normalized angle measure.

nodes.name: Niven's theorem
nodes.statement: For rational values of θ in degrees with 0 ≤ θ ≤ 90, the sine of θ degrees is rational only for θ = 0, 30 and 90, where the sine is 0, 1/2 and 1.
nodes.by: Ivan Niven, in his book Irrational Numbers; proven earlier by D. H. Lehmer, 1933, and by J. M. H. Olmstead
nodes.note: For rational θ, the only rational values of the sine or cosine are 0, ±1/2 and ±1. Niven extended Lehmer's result to the other trigonometric functions in 1956.

nodes.name: Legendre's equation
nodes.statement: Let a, b, c be nonzero, square-free, pairwise relatively prime integers that are not all positive and not all negative. Then ax² + by² + cz² = 0 has a solution in integers x, y, z, not all zero, if and only if −bc, −ca and −ab are quadratic residues modulo a, b and c, respectively.
nodes.by: Adrien-Marie Legendre, 1785
nodes.note: The equation is homogeneous, so a nonzero rational solution exists exactly when a nonzero integer solution does. Geometrically it asks for a rational point on a rational conic.

nodes.name: Abhyankar's lemma
nodes.statement: Let A, B, C be local fields such that A and B are finite extensions of C with ramification indices a and b. If B is tamely ramified over C and b divides a, then the compositum AB is an unramified extension of A.
nodes.by: Named after Shreeram Shankar Abhyankar
nodes.note: It allows one to kill tame ramification by taking an extension of a base field.

nodes.name: Agrawal's conjecture
nodes.statement: Let n and r be coprime positive integers. If (X − 1)ⁿ ≡ Xⁿ − 1 (mod n, X^r − 1), that is, the two polynomials agree after reducing coefficients mod n and the polynomials mod X^r − 1, then either n is prime or n² ≡ 1 (mod r).
nodes.by: Formulated by Rajat Bhattacharjee and Prashant Pandey in their 2001 thesis; attributed to Manindra Agrawal, 2002
nodes.note: If true, it would lower the runtime of the AKS primality test from Õ(log⁶ n) to Õ(log³ n). It has been checked by computer for r < 100 and n < 10¹⁰, but a heuristic argument by Carl Pomerance and Hendrik W. Lenstra suggests there are infinitely many counterexamples.

nodes.name: Albert–Brauer–Hasse–Noether theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a central simple algebra over an algebraic number field K. If A splits over every completion K_v of K, then A is a matrix algebra over K.
nodes.by: Richard Brauer, Helmut Hasse and Emmy Noether, and independently Abraham Adrian Albert
nodes.note: It is an example of a local-global principle and leads to a description of finite-dimensional division algebras over algebraic number fields in terms of their local invariants.

nodes.name: Artin–Verdier duality
nodes.statement: Let X be the spectrum of the ring of integers of a totally imaginary number field K, and F a constructible étale abelian sheaf on X. Then for every integer r, the Yoneda pairing H^r(X,F) × Ext^(3−r)(F, 𝔾ₘ) → H³(X, 𝔾ₘ) = ℚ/ℤ is a non-degenerate pairing of finite abelian groups.
nodes.by: Introduced by Verdier, 1964
nodes.note: It generalizes Tate duality and shows that, for étale cohomology, the ring of integers in a number field behaves like a 3-dimensional object. Deninger proved it in 1986 for constructible sheaves that need not be torsion.

nodes.name: Bhaskara's lemma
nodes.statement: Let m, x, y, N be integers and k a non-zero integer. If N x² + k = y², then N((mx + y)/k)² + (m² − N)/k = ((my + Nx)/k)².
nodes.note: It is used as a lemma in the chakravala method. It also holds for real or complex numbers, and when neither k nor m² − N is zero the implication goes in both directions.

nodes.name: Bogomolov conjecture
nodes.statement: Let C be a curve of genus g ≥ 2 defined over a number field K and embedded in its Jacobian J. Let ĥ be the Néron–Tate height on J associated with a symmetric ample line bundle. Then there is a number ε > 0 such that only finitely many points of C have height ĥ less than ε.
nodes.by: Named after Fedor Bogomolov; proved by Emmanuel Ullmo, 1998, and generalized to subvarieties of abelian varieties by Shou-Wu Zhang, 1998
nodes.note: It generalizes the Manin–Mumford conjecture by replacing torsion points with points of small Néron–Tate height. A point has height zero exactly when it is a torsion point.

nodes.name: Brauer–Siegel theorem
nodes.statement: Let K₁, K₂, … be number fields that are Galois extensions of ℚ, with discriminants D_i, class numbers h_i and regulators R_i. If [K_i : ℚ] / log|D_i| → 0 as i → ∞, then log(h_i R_i) / log √|D_i| → 1 as i → ∞. The Galois assumption can be dropped if all the degrees [K_i : ℚ] are bounded above by a uniform constant.
nodes.by: Richard Brauer and Carl Ludwig Siegel; Brauer's paper appeared in 1947
nodes.note: It generalizes results on class numbers of imaginary quadratic fields. The result is ineffective; effective results in the same direction began with Harold Stark in the early 1970s.

nodes.name: Brun–Titchmarsh theorem
nodes.statement: Let π(x;q,a) be the number of primes p ≤ x that are congruent to a modulo q. Then π(x;q,a) ≤ 2x / (φ(q) log(x/q)) for all q < x.
nodes.by: Proven by Montgomery and Vaughan using sieve methods; an earlier version by Brun and Titchmarsh had an extra factor 1 + o(1)
nodes.note: It is an upper bound on the distribution of prime numbers in arithmetic progressions. Motohashi (1973) gave a sharper bound when q ≤ x^(9/20).

nodes.name: Chowla–Mordell theorem
nodes.statement: Let p be an odd prime, χ a nontrivial Dirichlet character modulo p, and G(χ) = ∑ χ(a) ζᵃ its Gauss sum, where ζ is a primitive p-th root of unity in the complex numbers. Then G(χ)/|G(χ)| is a root of unity if and only if χ is the quadratic residue symbol modulo p.
nodes.by: Sarvadaman Chowla and Louis Mordell, independently, around 1951; the 'if' part was known to Gauss
nodes.note: It determines the cases where a Gauss sum is the square root of a prime number multiplied by a root of unity. The ratio in the theorem occurs in the functional equation of L-functions.

nodes.name: Carmichael's totient function conjecture
nodes.statement: For every positive integer n there is at least one other integer m ≠ n such that φ(m) = φ(n), where φ is Euler's totient function.
nodes.by: Robert Carmichael, 1907, who stated it as a theorem with a faulty proof; in 1922 he retracted the claim and stated it as an open problem
nodes.note: Kevin Ford determined in 1998 that any counterexample must be at least 10^(10^10).

nodes.name: Brocard's conjecture
nodes.statement: For every n ≥ 2, there are at least four prime numbers between (pₙ)² and (pₙ₊₁)², where pₙ is the n-th prime number.
nodes.by: Named after Henri Brocard
nodes.note: Legendre's conjecture, that there is a prime between consecutive integer squares, directly implies at least two primes between prime squares for pₙ ≥ 3.

nodes.name: Bézout's identity
nodes.statement: For any two integers a and b with greatest common divisor d, there are integers x and y such that ax + by = d. The greatest common divisor of 0 and 0 is taken to be 0.
nodes.by: Named after Étienne Bézout (1730–1783), who proved it for polynomials; the statement for integers appears earlier in the work of Claude Gaspard Bachet de Méziriac (1581–1638)
nodes.note: Euclid's lemma and the Chinese remainder theorem can be deduced from it. The identity also holds in every principal ideal domain.

nodes.name: Conductor–discriminant formula
nodes.statement: For a finite Galois extension L/K of global fields with Galois group G, the relative discriminant of L/K equals the product, over all irreducible characters χ of G, of the global Artin conductor 𝔣(χ) raised to the power χ(1).
nodes.by: Introduced by Hasse for abelian extensions and by Artin, 1931, for Galois extensions

nodes.name: Koukoulopoulos–Maynard theorem (Duffin–Schaeffer conjecture)
nodes.statement: Let f be a function from the positive integers to the positive reals. Then for almost all real α (with respect to Lebesgue measure), the inequality |α − p/q| < f(q)/q has infinitely many solutions in coprime integers p, q with q > 0 if and only if the sum over q ≥ 1 of φ(q)·f(q)/q diverges, where φ is Euler's totient function.
nodes.by: Proposed as a conjecture by R. J. Duffin and A. C. Schaeffer, 1941; proven by Dimitris Koukoulopoulos and James Maynard, 2019
nodes.note: That the approximations imply divergence of the series follows from the Borel–Cantelli lemma. The converse was the hard part.

nodes.name: Feit–Thompson conjecture
nodes.statement: There are no distinct prime numbers p and q such that (p^q − 1)/(p − 1) divides (q^p − 1)/(q − 1).
nodes.by: Suggested by Feit and Thompson, 1962
nodes.note: If true, it would greatly simplify the final chapter of the proof that every finite group of odd order is solvable. It is known for q = 2 and q = 3, while the stronger claim that the two numbers are always coprime fails for p = 17 and q = 3313.

nodes.name: Ferrero–Washington theorem
nodes.statement: Iwasawa's μ-invariant vanishes for cyclotomic Z_p-extensions of abelian algebraic number fields.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Iwasawa in 1971 for all Z_p-extensions and, after that failed, suggested by him for cyclotomic ones; proved by Ferrero and Washington, 1979; a different proof was given by Sinnott, 1984
nodes.note: Iwasawa had shown that the vanishing for cyclotomic Z_p-extensions of the rationals is equivalent to certain congruences between Bernoulli numbers, and Ferrero and Washington proved those congruences.

nodes.name: Firoozbakht's conjecture
nodes.statement: If pₙ is the n-th prime, then the n-th root of pₙ is a strictly decreasing function of n: the (n+1)-th root of pₙ₊₁ is less than the n-th root of pₙ for all n ≥ 1. Equivalently, pₙ₊₁ < pₙ^(1+1/n).
nodes.by: Farideh Firoozbakht, 1982
nodes.note: It has been verified for all primes below 2^64. If true, it would give a strong upper bound on gaps between consecutive primes.

nodes.name: Four exponentials conjecture
nodes.statement: If x₁, x₂ and y₁, y₂ are two pairs of complex numbers, with each pair linearly independent over the rational numbers, then at least one of the four numbers e^(x₁y₁), e^(x₁y₂), e^(x₂y₁), e^(x₂y₂) is transcendental.
nodes.by: Considered in the early 1940s by Atle Selberg, who never formally stated it; an equivalent statement was first mentioned in print by Theodor Schneider, 1957; Serge Lang and Kanakanahalli Ramachandra explicitly conjectured it in the 1960s
nodes.note: It would imply that there is no non-integer real number t such that both 2^t and 3^t are integers. The related six exponentials theorem is proven.

nodes.name: Friedlander–Iwaniec theorem
nodes.statement: There are infinitely many prime numbers of the form a² + b⁴, where a and b are integers.
nodes.by: John Friedlander and Henryk Iwaniec, 1997
nodes.note: Numbers of the form a² + b⁴ are very sparse: there are roughly X^(3/4) of them below X. The theorem does not settle whether infinitely many primes have the form a² + 1.

nodes.name: Fundamental theorem of ideal theory in number fields
nodes.statement: Every nonzero proper ideal in the ring of integers of a number field can be written uniquely as a product of nonzero prime ideals. Equivalently, every ring of integers of a number field is a Dedekind domain.

nodes.name: Rudin's conjecture
nodes.statement: For positive integers N, q, a, let Q(N; q, a) be the number of perfect squares among qn + a for n = 0, 1, …, N−1, and let Q(N) be the maximum of Q(N; q, a) over all q, a ≥ 1. The conjecture asserts that Q(N) = O(√N), and in its stronger form that Q(N) = Q(N; 24, 1) for N > 6.
nodes.by: Walter Rudin, 1960
nodes.note: It has applications in the theory of trigonometric series. Bombieri and Zannier proved Q(N) = O(N^(3/5+o(1))), and the strong form has been verified for 6 ≤ N ≤ 52.

nodes.name: Grunwald–Wang theorem
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, n a natural number and S a finite set of primes of K. Every element of K that is an nth power in the completion K_𝔭 for every prime 𝔭 outside S is an nth power in K, unless K is s-special for some s with 2^(s+1) dividing n and S contains every 2-adic prime 𝔭 for which K_𝔭 is s-special, where a field is s-special if it contains η_s = 2cos(2π/2^s) but none of i, η_(s+1) and i·η_(s+1); in that special case such elements form, modulo nth powers in K, a group of order 2.
nodes.by: Introduced by Grunwald, 1933, with a mistake that Wang found and corrected, 1948; Wang gave and proved the correct formulation in his 1950 thesis
nodes.note: It is a local-global principle. For K = ℚ the exception occurs only when 8 divides n and S contains 2: 16 is an 8th power in ℚ_p for every odd prime p but is not an 8th power in ℚ.

nodes.name: Hardy–Ramanujan theorem
nodes.statement: The normal order of ω(n), the number of distinct prime factors of n, is log log n. More precisely, for every real-valued function ψ(n) that tends to infinity as n tends to infinity, |ω(n) − log log n| < ψ(n)·√(log log n) holds for almost all positive integers n: the proportion of n below x for which it fails tends to 0 as x grows.
nodes.by: Proved by Ramanujan and checked by Hardy; a simple proof was later given by Pál Turán
nodes.note: Roughly, most numbers have about log log n distinct prime factors. The same holds for Ω(n), the number of prime factors counted with multiplicity, and the result is generalized by the Erdős–Kac theorem.

nodes.name: Hasse–Arf theorem
nodes.statement: Let L/K be a finite abelian Galois extension, where K has a discrete normalised valuation whose residue field has characteristic p > 0 and which extends uniquely to L. Then every jump of the upper numbering filtration G^t(L/K), t ≥ −1, of the ramification groups occurs at an integer.
nodes.by: A special case with finite residue fields was proved by Helmut Hasse; the general result was proved by Cahit Arf
nodes.note: For non-abelian extensions the jumps need not be integers. Jean-Pierre Serre gave an extension with Galois group the quaternion group of order 8 that has a jump at 3/2.

nodes.name: Hermite's identity
nodes.statement: For every real number x and every positive integer n, the sum of ⌊x + k/n⌋ for k = 0, 1, …, n−1 equals ⌊nx⌋, where ⌊ ⌋ denotes rounding down to the nearest integer.
nodes.by: Named after the French mathematician Charles Hermite

nodes.name: Hilbert's irreducibility theorem
nodes.statement: Let f₁, ..., fₙ be finitely many polynomials in the variables Y₁, ..., Yₛ whose coefficients are rational functions of X₁, ..., Xᵣ with rational coefficients, each irreducible over that field of rational functions. Then there are rational numbers a₁, ..., aᵣ such that, after substituting them for X₁, ..., Xᵣ, all of f₁, ..., fₙ remain irreducible as polynomials in Y₁, ..., Yₛ over ℚ.
nodes.by: David Hilbert, 1892
nodes.note: There are infinitely many such tuples, and integer values always suffice. Hilbert's original motivation was the inverse Galois problem, and the theorem is used as a step in Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem.

nodes.name: Honda–Tate theorem
nodes.statement: Let q be a power of a prime. Sending each simple abelian variety over the finite field with q elements to its Frobenius endomorphism gives a one-to-one correspondence between the isogeny classes of simple abelian varieties over that field and the conjugacy classes of Weil q-numbers. A Weil q-number is an algebraic integer all of whose conjugates have absolute value √q.
nodes.by: Tate, 1966 (the map is injective); Honda, 1968 (the map is surjective)
nodes.note: Since every abelian variety is isogenous to a product of simple ones, this classifies all abelian varieties over a finite field up to isogeny.

nodes.name: Hua's lemma
nodes.statement: Let P be an integral-valued polynomial of degree k, let ε be a positive real number, and let f(α) = ∑ from x = 1 to N of exp(2πiP(x)α). Then the integral from 0 to 1 of |f(α)|^λ dα is at most a constant depending on P and ε times N raised to the power μ(λ), where the point (λ, μ(λ)) lies on the polygonal line with vertices (2^ν, 2^ν − ν + ε) for ν = 1, …, k.
nodes.by: Named after Hua Loo-keng

nodes.name: Goormaghtigh conjecture
nodes.statement: Apart from exchanging the two sides, the equation (xᵐ − 1)/(x − 1) = (yⁿ − 1)/(y − 1), with distinct integers x and y larger than one and exponents m and n larger than two, has only two solutions: (5³ − 1)/(5 − 1) = (2⁵ − 1)/(2 − 1) = 31 and (90³ − 1)/(90 − 1) = (2¹³ − 1)/(2 − 1) = 8191. Equivalently, 31 and 8191 are the only numbers that are repunits with at least three digits in two different bases.
nodes.by: Named for the Belgian mathematician René Goormaghtigh
nodes.note: Davenport, Lewis and Schinzel showed in 1961 that for fixed m and n there are only finitely many solutions. Yuan showed in 2005 that for m = 3 and odd n there are no solutions other than the two known ones.

nodes.name: Sums of three cubes problem
nodes.statement: Every integer that is not congruent to 4 or 5 modulo 9 can be written as a sum of three cubes of integers, where negative cubes are allowed.
nodes.note: The condition is necessary, because cubes modulo 9 are 0, 1 and −1, and no three of these sum to 4 or 5 modulo 9. In 1992 Roger Heath-Brown conjectured that every such integer has infinitely many representations.

nodes.name: Bertrand's postulate
nodes.statement: For every integer n > 3 there is at least one prime p with n < p < 2n − 2. A weaker form says that for every n > 1 there is a prime p with n < p < 2n.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Joseph Bertrand, 1845, who verified it for all integers up to 3,000,000; proved by Chebyshev, 1852
nodes.note: It is also called the Bertrand–Chebyshev theorem. It is weaker than the prime number theorem but makes precise claims for small values of n.

nodes.name: Katz–Lang finiteness theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a smooth, geometrically connected scheme of finite type over a field K that is finitely generated over the prime field, and let Ker(X/K) be the kernel of the maps between their abelianized fundamental groups. Then Ker(X/K) is finite if K has characteristic 0, and the part of the kernel coprime to p is finite if K has characteristic p > 0.
nodes.by: Nick Katz and Serge Lang, 1981

nodes.name: Scholz conjecture
nodes.statement: For every positive integer n, l(2ⁿ − 1) ≤ n − 1 + l(n), where l(n) is the length of the shortest addition chain producing n. An addition chain is a sequence of numbers starting with 1 in which every later number is a sum of two earlier ones (which may be equal), and its length is the number of sums needed.
nodes.by: Arnold Scholz, 1937; Alfred Brauer studied it soon afterward and proved a weaker bound
nodes.note: If true, it would give short addition chains for the Mersenne numbers. Neill Clift has announced an example showing the bound is not always tight.

nodes.name: Krasner's lemma
nodes.statement: Let (K, v) be a Henselian valued field, let f be a monic polynomial of degree n > 1 with coefficients in K and roots α₁, …, αₙ in an algebraic closure of K, and let β lie in that algebraic closure. If v(β − α₁) > v(α₁ − αⱼ) for every j ≠ 1, so that β is closer to α₁ than any other root is, then α₁ lies in the field K(β).
nodes.note: It can be used to show that ℂ_p, the completion of the algebraic closure of ℚ_p, is algebraically closed. A generalization replaces β by the roots of a polynomial g of any degree close to a group of roots of f.

nodes.name: Kummer's theorem
nodes.statement: For integers n ≥ m ≥ 0 and a prime p, the exponent of the highest power of p dividing the binomial coefficient C(n, m) equals the number of carries when m is added to n − m in base p.
nodes.by: Ernst Kummer, 1852
nodes.note: An equivalent form: this exponent equals (S_p(m) + S_p(n − m) − S_p(n)) / (p − 1), where S_p is the sum of base-p digits. It can be proved from Legendre's formula.

nodes.name: Landau prime ideal theorem
nodes.statement: For any number field K, the number of prime ideals of K with norm at most X is asymptotic to X/log X.
nodes.by: Edmund Landau, 1903
nodes.note: It generalizes the prime number theorem to number fields. A more precise estimate is Li(X) + O_K(X exp(−c_K √log X)), where c_K is a constant depending on K.

nodes.name: Latimer–MacDuffee theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a monic polynomial of degree n with integer coefficients that is irreducible. There is a one-to-one correspondence between ℤ-similarity classes of n×n integer matrices with characteristic polynomial f and the ideal classes of the order ℤ[x]/(f(x)), where two ideals are equivalent if they are equal up to a nonzero rational scalar multiple.
nodes.by: Claiborne Latimer and Cyrus Colton MacDuffee, 1933
nodes.note: An order in a number field has only finitely many ideal classes, so there are only finitely many conjugacy classes of integer matrices with characteristic polynomial f. Olga Taussky-Todd later made significant contributions to its theory.

nodes.name: Bombieri–Lang conjecture
nodes.statement: If X is a positive-dimensional algebraic variety of general type defined over a number field k, then the k-rational points of X do not form a dense set in the Zariski topology.
nodes.by: Enrico Bombieri (lecture at the University of Chicago, 1980) and Serge Lang (papers starting in 1971), posed independently
nodes.note: A weak form concerns smooth surfaces of general type, and a refined form asks for a dense open subset with only finitely many rational points over every number field extension of k. If true, the conjecture would resolve the Erdős–Ulam problem.

nodes.name: Davenport–Erdős theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a sequence of positive integers and M(A) the set of all products ka with k a positive integer and a in A. Then the lower natural density of M(A), its logarithmic density (where each element a has weight 1/a), and its sequential density (the limit of the densities of the sets of multiples of the first i elements of A) all give the same number.
nodes.by: Harold Davenport and Paul Erdős, 1936
nodes.note: A sequence A for which these densities of M(A) equal one is called a Behrend sequence.

nodes.name: Hilbert–Waring theorem
nodes.statement: For each natural number k there is a positive integer s such that every natural number is the sum of at most s natural numbers raised to the power k.
nodes.by: Proposed by Edward Waring, 1770; proved by Hilbert, 1909
nodes.note: For example, every natural number is the sum of at most 4 squares, 9 cubes, or 19 fourth powers.

nodes.name: Kummer–Vandiver conjecture
nodes.statement: For every prime p, p does not divide the class number of the maximal real subfield ℚ(ζ_p)⁺ of the p-th cyclotomic field.
nodes.by: Ernst Kummer, in letters to Leopold Kronecker, 1849 and 1853; independently rediscovered around 1920 by Philipp Furtwängler and Harry Vandiver
nodes.note: Kummer showed that if p does not divide the class number of the cyclotomic field ℚ(ζ_p), then Fermat's Last Theorem holds for exponent p. The conjecture has been checked by computer for primes below 2^31.

nodes.name: Littlewood conjecture
nodes.statement: For every pair of real numbers α and β, the limit inferior as n → ∞ of n·‖nα‖·‖nβ‖ is 0, where ‖x‖ is the distance from x to the nearest integer.
nodes.by: J. E. Littlewood, around 1930
nodes.note: It holds if either number is rational or not badly approximable. In 2006 Einsiedler, Katok and Lindenstrauss proved that the set of counterexamples has Hausdorff dimension zero.

nodes.name: Lonely runner conjecture
nodes.statement: Suppose n runners start together at the same point of a circular track of unit length and run with constant speeds that are all distinct from one another (speeds may be negative). Then each runner is lonely at some time, meaning at distance at least 1/n along the circle from every other runner.
nodes.by: Posed in 1967 by Jörg M. Wills in number-theoretic terms, and independently as a view-obstruction problem in 1974 by Thomas W. Cusick
nodes.note: The conjecture is known to be true for 13 runners or fewer. It implies solutions to view-obstruction problems and bounds related to chromatic numbers of certain graphs.

nodes.name: Mahler's compactness theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be the space GLₙ(ℝ)/GLₙ(ℤ) of lattices in ℝⁿ with its quotient topology, and let Δ be the absolute value of the determinant. A subset Y of X is relatively compact if and only if Δ is bounded on Y and there is a neighbourhood N of 0 in ℝⁿ such that, for every lattice Λ in Y, the only lattice point of Λ in N is 0.
nodes.by: Mahler, 1946
nodes.note: A lattice can degenerate in only two ways: its fundamental domain gets ever larger volume, or it contains shorter and shorter vectors. David Mumford generalized it to semisimple Lie groups.

nodes.name: Maier's theorem
nodes.statement: Let π be the prime-counting function and λ > 1. Then (π(x + (log x)^λ) − π(x)) / (log x)^(λ−1) has no limit as x tends to infinity: its limit superior is greater than 1 and its limit inferior is less than 1.
nodes.by: Helmut Maier
nodes.note: Cramér's probabilistic model of primes incorrectly predicts that this ratio has limit 1 when λ ≥ 2.

nodes.name: Main conjecture of Iwasawa theory
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime, F_n = ℚ(ζ) with ζ a root of unity of order p^(n+1), H_∞ the inverse limit of the p-power parts of the ideal class groups of the F_n, and V = H_∞ ⊗ ℚ_p. If i is an odd integer not congruent to 1 mod p − 1, then the characteristic polynomial h_p(ω^i, T) of a topological generator γ of Γ acting on the ω^i-eigenspace of V (ω the Teichmüller character) and the power series G_p(ω^(1−i), T), defined from the p-adic L-function by G_p(ω^j, u^s − 1) = L_p(ω^j, s), generate the same ideal of the power series ring ℤ_p[[T]].
nodes.by: Proved by Kenkichi Iwasawa for primes satisfying the Kummer–Vandiver conjecture, and for all primes by Barry Mazur and Andrew Wiles
nodes.note: The Herbrand–Ribet theorem and the Gras conjecture are both easy consequences of it. Wiles later proved it for all totally real number fields.

nodes.name: Manin–Drinfeld theorem
nodes.statement: The difference of two cusps of a modular curve has finite order in the Jacobian variety.
nodes.by: Manin, 1972, and Drinfeld, 1973

nodes.name: Meyer's theorem
nodes.statement: An indefinite quadratic form Q with rational coefficients in five or more variables nontrivially represents zero over the rationals. In other words, if Q = 0 has a non-zero real solution, then it has a non-zero rational solution, and by clearing denominators an integral one.
nodes.note: The number of variables is best possible, since some indefinite rational quadratic forms in four variables do not represent zero. The theorem is usually deduced from the Hasse–Minkowski theorem, which was proved later.

nodes.name: Néron–Ogg–Shafarevich criterion
nodes.statement: Let A be an elliptic curve or abelian variety over a local field K, and let ℓ be a prime not dividing the characteristic of the residue field of K. Then A has good reduction if and only if the ℓ-adic Tate module of A is unramified.
nodes.by: Andrew Ogg introduced it for elliptic curves; Jean-Pierre Serre and John Tate used results of André Néron to extend it to abelian varieties
nodes.note: Serre and Tate named it after Ogg, Néron and Igor Shafarevich, since Ogg's result seems to have been known to Shafarevich.

nodes.name: Oppenheim conjecture
nodes.statement: Let Q be a real nondegenerate indefinite quadratic form in n ≥ 3 variables that is not a multiple of a form with rational coefficients. Then for any ε > 0 there is a non-zero vector x with integer components such that |Q(x)| < ε.
nodes.by: Conjectured for n ≥ 5 by Alexander Oppenheim, 1929; the stronger version is due to Harold Davenport, 1946; proved in complete generality by Grigory Margulis, 1987
nodes.note: The conjecture is also stated as saying that the values of such a form on integer vectors are dense in the real line. Margulis proved it with methods of ergodic theory, and it suffices to treat the case n = 3.

nodes.name: Selberg's zeta function conjecture
nodes.statement: Fix ε with 0 < ε < 0.001 and let H = T^(27/82 + ε), where 27/82 = 1/3 − 1/246. Then there is a constant c > 0 such that for every sufficiently large T, there are at least cH ln T real numbers t between T and T + H with ζ(1/2 + it) = 0.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Atle Selberg, who had proved the case of exponent 0.5 + ε in 1942; proved by Anatolii Karatsuba, 1984
nodes.note: Selberg conjectured that the exponent 0.5 in H = T^(0.5+ε) can be lowered. The estimates of Selberg and Karatsuba cannot be improved in the order of growth as T → ∞.

nodes.name: Siegel's theorem on integral points
nodes.statement: Let C be an affine algebraic curve defined over a number field K, let g be the genus of the smooth projective curve birational to C, and let n be the number of points at infinity of C. If g ≥ 1, or g = 0 and n ≥ 3, then C has only finitely many points whose coordinates lie in the ring of integers of K, and more generally only finitely many S-integral points.
nodes.by: Carl Ludwig Siegel, 1929
nodes.note: The proof is ineffective: it shows the set of integral points is finite but gives no method for finding them. It was the first major result on Diophantine equations that depended only on the genus of the curve.

nodes.name: Roth's theorem
nodes.statement: Every irrational algebraic number α has irrationality exponent equal to 2. That is, for every ε > 0, the inequality |α − p/q| < 1/q^(2+ε) has only finitely many solutions in coprime integers p and q.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Siegel; proved by Roth, 1955
nodes.note: It gives the best possible bound, culminating earlier bounds by Liouville (1844), Thue (1909), Siegel (1921) and Dyson (1947). The theorem is not effective: no bound is known on the possible values of p and q.

nodes.name: Lagrange's four-square theorem
nodes.statement: Every nonnegative integer can be written as a sum of four squares of integers, n = a² + b² + c² + d².
nodes.by: Stated by Claude Gaspard Bachet de Méziriac, 1621; proved by Joseph-Louis Lagrange, 1770
nodes.note: Diophantus was already aware of the theorem from examples in the Arithmetica. It is a special case of the Fermat polygonal number theorem and of Waring's problem.

nodes.name: Star of David theorem
nodes.statement: In Pascal's triangle, the two triangles of binomial coefficients that form the Star of David shape around an entry have equal greatest common divisors: gcd{C(n−1, k−1), C(n, k+1), C(n+1, k)} = gcd{C(n−1, k), C(n, k−1), C(n+1, k+1)}.
nodes.by: Henry W. Gould, 1972
nodes.note: The two sets of three binomial coefficients also have equal products.

nodes.name: Størmer's theorem
nodes.statement: For every finite set P of primes, there are only finitely many pairs of consecutive P-smooth numbers. Here the P-smooth numbers are the integers that are products of primes from P.
nodes.by: Named after Carl Størmer, who gave a procedure for finding all such pairs using Pell equations
nodes.note: Finiteness also follows from the Thue–Siegel–Roth theorem, but Størmer's method finds all the pairs.

nodes.name: Subspace theorem
nodes.statement: Let L_1, ..., L_n be linearly independent linear forms in n variables with algebraic coefficients, and let ε > 0 be a real number. Then the non-zero integer points x with |L_1(x)⋯L_n(x)| < |x|^(−ε) lie in a finite number of proper subspaces of ℚⁿ.
nodes.by: Schmidt, 1972; generalised by Schlickewei, 1977, to more general absolute values on number fields
nodes.note: In words, points of small height in projective space lie in a finite number of hyperplanes. The case n = 1 of its corollary on Diophantine approximation is the Thue–Siegel–Roth theorem.

nodes.name: Tate duality
nodes.statement: For a p-adic local field k, a finite group scheme M and its dual M′ = Hom(M, 𝔾ₘ), there is a perfect pairing of finite groups Hʳ(k,M) × H²⁻ʳ(k,M′) → H²(k,𝔾ₘ) = ℚ/ℤ, where 𝔾ₘ is the multiplicative group.
nodes.by: John Tate, 1962; Georges Poitou, 1967
nodes.note: Similar versions hold for local fields of characteristic p > 0 and for Archimedean fields. A global version over number fields is called Poitou–Tate duality.

nodes.name: Turán–Kubilius inequality
nodes.statement: Let f be an additive complex-valued arithmetic function, and put A(x) = ∑ f(p^ν) p^(−ν) (1 − 1/p) and B(x)² = ∑ |f(p^ν)|² p^(−ν), both sums over all prime powers p^ν ≤ x with ν ≥ 1. Then there is a function ε(x) tending to 0 as x tends to infinity such that for every x ≥ 2, (1/x) ∑_(n ≤ x) |f(n) − A(x)|² ≤ (2 + ε(x)) B(x)².
nodes.by: Pál Turán, 1934 (special case); generalized by Jonas Kubilius, 1956 and 1964
nodes.note: It is useful for proving results about the normal order of an arithmetic function. Turán developed it to give a simpler proof of the Hardy–Ramanujan theorem on the number of distinct prime divisors.

nodes.name: Vaughan's identity
nodes.statement: For any positive numbers U and V and every positive integer n, the von Mangoldt function satisfies Λ(n) = a₁(n) + a₂(n) + a₃(n) + a₄(n), where a₁(n) = Λ(n) for n ≤ U and 0 for n > U, a₂(n) = −∑ Λ(m)μ(d) over all mdr = n with m ≤ U and d ≤ V, a₃(n) = ∑ μ(d) log h over all hd = n with d ≤ V, and a₄(n) = −∑ Λ(m)·(∑ μ(d) over divisors d of k with d ≤ V) over all mk = n with m > U and k > 1. Here μ is the Möbius function.
nodes.by: Vaughan, 1977
nodes.note: It is used to estimate sums of f(n)Λ(n) over n ≤ N, and it simplified Vinogradov's work on trigonometric sums and the proof of the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem. Heath-Brown generalized it in 1982.

nodes.name: Vojta's conjecture
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field, X a non-singular algebraic variety over F, D an effective divisor on X with at worst normal crossings, H an ample divisor and K a canonical divisor on X; choose Weil heights h_H and h_K, a local height λᵥ for D at each absolute value v of F, a finite set S of absolute values of F, and ε > 0. Then there are a constant C and a non-empty Zariski open set U ⊆ X such that the sum of λᵥ(P) over v in S, plus h_K(P), is at most ε·h_H(P) + C for every point P of U with coordinates in F.
nodes.by: Introduced by Paul Vojta
nodes.note: It was motivated by an analogy between diophantine approximation and Nevanlinna theory in complex analysis. It implies many other conjectures in Diophantine approximation, Diophantine equations, arithmetic geometry, and mathematical logic.

nodes.name: Weil's conjecture on Tamagawa numbers
nodes.statement: The Tamagawa number τ(G) of a simply connected simple algebraic group G defined over a number field is 1.
nodes.by: Observed by Weil, 1959; the proof was completed by V. I. Chernousov, 1989, building on Langlands (1966), Lai (1980) and Kottwitz (1988)
nodes.note: In 2011 Lurie and Gaitsgory announced a proof for algebraic groups over function fields over finite fields.

nodes.name: Zsigmondy's theorem
nodes.statement: Let a > b > 0 be coprime integers. For every integer n ≥ 1 other than 1, 2 and 6, there is a prime p that divides aⁿ − bⁿ but does not divide aᵏ − bᵏ for any positive integer k < n.
nodes.by: Karl Zsigmondy, 1892
nodes.note: Such a prime is called a primitive prime divisor. Similarly, aⁿ + bⁿ has at least one primitive prime divisor, with the single exception 2³ + 1³ = 9.

nodes.name: Collatz conjecture
nodes.statement: Start with any positive integer. If the current number is even, halve it; if it is odd, multiply it by 3 and add 1. Repeating this always eventually reaches 1, whichever positive integer is chosen to start.
nodes.by: Lothar Collatz, 1937
nodes.note: It is one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics. It has been checked by computer for all starting values up to 2^71, but no general proof has been found.

nodes.name: Brun's theorem
nodes.statement: The sum of the reciprocals of the twin primes converges to a finite value, known as Brun's constant.
nodes.by: Viggo Brun, 1919
nodes.note: It has historical importance in the introduction of sieve methods. Because the sum converges, it does not settle whether there are infinitely many twin primes.

nodes.name: Erdős–Kac theorem
nodes.statement: Let ω(n) be the number of distinct prime factors of n. For any fixed a < b, the proportion of integers n ≤ x for which (ω(n) − log log n)/√(log log n) lies between a and b tends, as x → ∞, to (1/√(2π)) ∫ from a to b of e^(−t²/2) dt, the area under the standard normal curve between a and b.
nodes.by: Named after Paul Erdős and Mark Kac; the proof is due to Erdős
nodes.note: It is an extension of the Hardy–Ramanujan theorem and is also known as the fundamental theorem of probabilistic number theory.

nodes.name: Kronecker's approximation theorem
nodes.statement: Given real vectors α_1, …, α_m and β in ℝⁿ, the vector β can be approximated arbitrarily closely by sums ∑ q_i α_i − p with integers q_i and an integer vector p, if and only if for every integer vector r with ∑_j α_ij r_j an integer for each i, the number ∑_j β_j r_j is also an integer. For m = n = 1: for any irrational α, any real β and any ε > 0 there are integers p and q with q > 0 such that |αq − p − β| < ε.
nodes.by: Leopold Kronecker, 1884
nodes.note: It generalizes Dirichlet's approximation theorem to multiple variables.

nodes.name: Midy's theorem
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime and a/p a fraction between 0 and 1 whose decimal expansion repeats with a shortest repeating block of even length 2n. Then each digit in the second half of the block and the corresponding digit in the first half add up to 9, so the two n-digit halves add up to 10ⁿ − 1.
nodes.by: Named after the French mathematician E. Midy, whose paper on periodic decimal fractions appeared in 1836
nodes.note: For example, 1/7 = 0.142857… and 142 + 857 = 999. The theorem and its extension hold in any base b, with 10ⁿ − 1 replaced by bⁿ − 1.

nodes.name: Rosser's theorem
nodes.statement: For every n ≥ 1, the nth prime number pₙ is greater than n log n, where log is the natural logarithm.
nodes.by: J. Barkley Rosser, 1939
nodes.note: In 1999 Pierre Dusart proved a tighter bound: pₙ > n(log n + log log n − 1) for n ≥ 2.

nodes.name: Bonse's inequality
nodes.statement: For every n ≥ 4, if p₁, …, pₙ, pₙ₊₁ are the first n+1 prime numbers, then the product p₁p₂⋯pₙ of the first n primes is greater than pₙ₊₁².
nodes.by: Named after H. Bonse
nodes.note: It relates the size of a primorial to the smallest prime that does not appear in its prime factorization.

nodes.name: Fermat's theorem on sums of two squares
nodes.statement: An odd prime p can be written as p = x² + y² with x and y integers if and only if p ≡ 1 (mod 4).
nodes.by: First observed by Albert Girard, published 1625; stated by Fermat in a letter to Marin Mersenne, 1640; first proved by Euler, 1749
nodes.note: Applied to prime factorizations, it shows that a positive integer is a sum of two squares if and only if every prime factor congruent to 3 modulo 4 occurs to an even exponent. Fermat gave no proof, and Euler found the first one by infinite descent.

nodes.name: Thue's lemma
nodes.statement: Let a and m be integers with m > 1, and let X and Y be positive integers with X ≤ m < XY. Then there are integers x and y such that ay ≡ x (mod m), |x| < X and 0 < y < Y.
nodes.by: First known proof attributed to Axel Thue, using a pigeonhole argument
nodes.note: Taking m to be a prime p congruent to 1 modulo 4 gives a proof of Fermat's theorem on sums of two squares.

nodes.name: Newman's conjecture
nodes.statement: For any integers m and r with 0 ≤ r ≤ m−1, the partition function p(n) satisfies p(n) ≡ r (mod m) for infinitely many non-negative integers n.
nodes.by: Morris Newman, 1960
nodes.note: Newman proved the cases m = 5 and 13, and later m = 65. Ahlgren and Boylan extended it to all primes except possibly 3, and then to all prime powers except powers of 2 or 3.

nodes.name: Gelfond–Schneider theorem
nodes.statement: If a and b are algebraic numbers (real or complex) with a not equal to 0 or 1 and b not rational, then every value of aᵇ is a transcendental number.
nodes.by: Aleksandr Gelfond and Theodor Schneider, independently, 1934
nodes.note: It answers Hilbert's seventh problem affirmatively. It shows, for example, that 2^√2 and e^π are transcendental.

nodes.name: Lifting-the-exponent lemma
nodes.statement: Let p be an odd prime and let ν_p(x) be the exponent of the highest power of p dividing x. If x and y are integers not divisible by p, n is a positive integer, and p divides x − y, then ν_p(xⁿ − yⁿ) = ν_p(x − y) + ν_p(n).
nodes.by: Some ideas appeared in the work of Édouard Lucas by 1878; modern systematic formulation first published by Mihai Manea, 2006
nodes.note: This is the main case. The lemma also has formulas for sums xⁿ + yⁿ and for p = 2. It is related to Hensel's lemma and is often used in mathematical olympiads.
